articles.summary: ⚽ Premier League updates from the 12.30pm BST kick-off ⚽ Live scoreboard | Tables | Top scorers | Email Scott Everton make two changes in the wake of their 2-2 draw at Hull City. articles.content:
Everton make two changes in the wake of their 2-2 draw at Hull City. Merlin Röhl and Vitalii Mykolenko replace Micheal Keane and Brennan Johnson, the latter dropping to the bench.

Chelsea meanwhile make one change to the starting XI sent out to thrash Bournemouth 5-1 last weekend. Jorrel Hato comes into the defence at the expense of Pep Chavarría.

Everton: Pickford, Maitland-Niles, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko, Garner, Armstrong, Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall, Grealish, Barry. Subs: Travers, O’Brien, George, Dibling, Johnson, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Graham.

Chelsea: Martinez, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Pedro Neto, Henderson, Caicedo, Hato, Palmer, Rogers, Joao Pedro. Subs: Penders, Palestra, Fofana, Barco, Welbeck, Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao, Lavia.

Fifth plays sixth at the Hill Dickinson this lunchtime, in a fixture that isn’t so easy to predict. Chelsea have quickly established an identity under Xabi Alonso as the great entertainers: they’ve scored 15 goals in six matches, with 13 whistling in down the other end. Their last two results – a 3-0 loss at Brentford followed by a 5-1 rout of Bournemouth – illustrate what they’re all about right now. Everton are similarly difficult to pin down, veering between doughty low-scoring shut-out wins (2-0 Palace, 1-0 Ipswich) and rollercoaster 2-2 draws (Manchester United and Hull City, Ainsley Maitland-Niles the centre of attention in both games, for wildly different reasons). The Toffees also remain undefeated, no small feat when you consider the downcast mood around the club at the end of an unsuccessful transfer window.

Throw in the fact that Chelsea don’t particularly like coming to visit the blue half of Merseyside – they’ve lost 2-0 and 3-0 on two of their most recent three visits, the other being a goalless draw – and so while they go into this match as favourites, you wouldn’t exactly risk the farm on it. This could be great fun. Kick-off is at 12.30pm BST. It’s on!

articles.title: Farke backs under-fire Carrick, Mourinho defends ‘disrespected’ Vinícius, and Premier League buildup – matchday live
articles.summary: ⚽️ News, discussion and buildup to Saturday’s action ⚽️ Premier League: 10 things to look out for | Mail us Fun and games in Spain… Real Madrid have again demanded the resignation of the president of La Liga after he compared the club’s efforts to discredit referees with the propaganda techniques of Nazi Germany. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho has said if he were winger Vinicius Junior he would have left the club this summer.

The Brazilian was sent off during Madrid’s win over Villarreal last weekend for hair pulling and was banned for four matches, meaning he will miss the Clasico against Barcelona on 25 October. Vinicius, 26, has also been targeted regularly by opposition fans and been racially abused on many occasions since joining Madrid in 2018.

“He’s a spectacular kid who it’s easy to have a good relationship with,” Mourinho told reporters. He’s a fantastic boy, tremendous credit to him for the fact that he keeps living and surviving and still having a smile.

“If it were me in his place, probably I wouldn’t be here. In this last summer I would have forced an exit to a league, a country, to somewhere there are rival clubs and stadiums that respect him.” Agence France-Presse

Our first football liveblog of the weekend is up and running, team news from Everton v Chelsea with Scott Murray shortly:

Cristiano Ronaldo grabbed the scarf in the colours of the Saudi Arabian flag and waved it at the sparse but enthusiastic crowd, who responded with rapturous cheers. It was a gesture of defiance rather than a victory salute, encapsulating the Saudi equivalent of “Keep calm and carry on”.

Monday night’s Asian Champions League Elite game between Al-Nassr and the Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana had ended with a 3-1 win for the Saudi club coached by Ange Postecoglou, with Ronaldo, supported by Sadio Mané, scoring, the smattering of star names indicative of the lure of the Saudi Pro League. Yet this isn’t quite how Ronaldo and co would have anticipated life in Riyadh. The meagre attendance aside, Monday’s game was delayed by a threat of missile attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels. A safety warning issued 15 minutes before kick-off came two days after 13 people died and more than 300 were wounded by Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport.

William Hargreaves has emailed in on my question earlier about Arsenal’s start in the WSL: ”You pose an interesting question: why are Renée Slegers’ team struggling? A simple answer is that they’re not scoring enough. A more complex answer might have to begin by asking what lay behind her initial success? As is frequently the case, a managerial change gives the new coach the opportunity to build on what has been accomplished. (I remember wondering how much of Leicester City’s magnificent year under Ranieri was a result of what went before under Nigel Pearson?)

“It might be that Renée was the perfect foil for Eideval, who might have become the wrong man, possibly experienced fracture or dysfunction within the squad, but who had put together a great group of players and coached great skills. It just needed redirecting to release potential and win. Renée released this capability. But now that rebuilding is required, how well placed is she? They lost talent over the summer and recruited more. Maybe they just need time to gel?

Real Madrid have again demanded the resignation of the president of La Liga after he compared the club’s efforts to discredit referees with the propaganda techniques of Nazi Germany.

Javier Tebas lashed out at Madrid on Friday on social media with a long post that criticised how its club television channel says referees hurt its chances of winning. The channel regularly runs reels of what it considers gross errors by match officials who are set to work upcoming games for the 15-time European champions.

Tebas compared the tactic with those used by Joseph Goebbels, the minister of propaganda in Nazi Germany during the second world war. “The executive of Real Madrid has an orchestra of mouthpieces and Real Madrid leads the way,” Tebas wrote. “Its script is always the same: select plays that favor it, repeat the alleged affront, increase suspicion and name enemies. It reminds one of the propaganda techniques that Goebbels used.”

Tebas added: “The comparison is with the techniques, not with the ideology or, of course, with Madrid fans.”

Michael Carrick returned his most impressive performance precisely when required as he took questions in the midst of the first crisis engulfing him as Manchester United’s manager.

His team are bombing in the league after the club’s poorest start since 1986 and out of the Carabao Cup, and after Tuesday’s Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid Lisandro Martínez showed up ruptures at United by calling out the director of football, Jason Wilcox.

All of this two months into a first full campaign piloting United after last term ended so rosily for the former United midfielder.

On the final day of last season, United won 3-0 at Brighton and Carrick secured an impressive third-place finish, 48 hours after agreeing a two-year deal to continue as head coach.

By last Saturday, United had six points from the first six games after drawing 1-1 with Tottenham at Old Trafford, placing Carrick’s job in jeopardy as the walls closed in on him a fortnight before the clocks go back.

Read Jamie Jackson’s full analysis of the latest drama at United here:

There is only one fixture in the WSL today, that’s 12.45pm BST kick-off at the Emirates between Arsenal and Birminham. It’s been a slow start to the season for the Gunners, who are currently 10th in the table, and only a few spots above the Blues. There was a further blow for Arsenal this week with the news that key midfielder Mariona Caldentey would miss about two months of action because of a hamstring injury. Why are Renée Slegers struggling? If you have any thoughts on that or anything else WSL-related drop me an email via the link at the top of the page.

Daniel Farke has jumped to the defence of Michael Carrick, claiming the under-fire Manchester United boss has done “an amazing job”.

Carrick delivered Champions League football via a third-placed finish last season after replacing Ruben Amorim on an interim basis in January and was rewarded in May with a permanent two-year contract. However, the former Middlesbrough manager has come under mounting pressure following United’s poor start to the season and Farke said it is undeserved.

The German, whose side face the Reds at Elland Road on Sunday, said: “We don’t have too many young British managers in the Premier League, and right now we have someone, a really promising young manager, who has done for me an excellent job at Middlesbrough, and he came in (at United) last season.

“[He] has helped a lot to stabilise the club, more or less like to steady the ship, and has done amazing job and right now, after six gamedays … the criticism starts already. I don’t like it. If we have young, promising managers, come on, let’s look after them a bit, especially if they have a British passport.”

Farke, who jokingly described himself as “half-British”, added: “When you keep in mind what he has done for the club for many years as a player, what he has done last season, where many people would have been hesitant … he has done a tremendous job.

“I like it when young British managers come through and for that, I don’t see why there’s so much negativity. I think we should be happy that we have someone with so much potential and don’t question them too early.” Press Association

The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman. I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.

The former Republic of Ireland international has been speaking to Donald McRae about on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career:

Burnley 1-2 Wolves: Wolves extend Burnley’s home woes to a full year as Vardy strikes in vain

There was some Friday night domestic action, in what would have been a Premier League fixture last season, as Wolves came from 1-0 down to beat Burnley 2-1 at Turf Moor. Jamie Vardy got his first goal of the season to open the scoring for the Clarets, but Fernando Lopez and Tawanda Chirewa saw Wolves secure the three points that took them up into the playoff places.

Speaking ahead of the 12.30pm kick-off on Merseyside, Xabi Alonso has been speaking about the need for his porous defence to tighten up. Chelsea have shipped 13 goals already this season, more than double what their opponents Everton have let in.

Alonso is also dealing with the absence of Reece James for three months after the defender underwent knee surgery after picking up an injury in training. In the absence of his captain, Alonso is determined to build on Chelsea’s strong display in 5-1 win over Bournemouth last weekend at the Hill Dickinson against Everton.

“You need a lot of clean sheets to win trophies,” he said. “But you [also] need to score a lot of goals. So it’s about being strong in defence, being good in attack and we are in that process. We are still early days; to do a very deep analysis, it’s too early. We can maybe talk in February. Those tweaks … they need to come naturally and we are not in that moment yet.

“The obsession is to win and to compete in the best possible way. The clean sheets will come, I’m pretty sure of that, because we want to play with good balance and good control.”

Meanwhile David Moyes believes Jordan Pickford will relish the challenge to his England place from James Trafford and remains the nation’s undisputed No 1 goalkeeper.

Pickford and Trafford shared goalkeeping duties during the recent four-game international break as part of an arranged plan by manager Thomas Tuchel. The 24-year-old Leeds player is considered the biggest threat to emerge to Pickford’s long-held position with the national team but Moyes insists the Everton keeper has been sharper than ever this season.

“When Jordan came back from the World Cup, it might be the best I have ever seen him,” the Everton manager said. “He was lean, he was sharp, his footwork was brilliant, he was fast across the goal and if you look at some of the saves he has made between now and then he has made a couple of brilliant, brilliant saves.

“I spoke to him when he came back and said: ‘You know you have a bit of competition now with Trafford, how are you going to deal with it?’ I don’t see Jordan falling away at the moment. I think if it really mattered to England then Jordan would still be the one who was there because he makes saves. He did that in the Argentina game. He has that experience and he is not ageing.”

Check out the talk, for more from the Premier League managers ahead of the weekend fixtures:

Looking to the Championship a few games stand out, we have early leaders Swansea welcoming West Ham to south Wales and third plays fourth as Birmingham City take on QPR at St Andrew’s.

Good morning, another Premier League weekend is upon us, kicking off with an intriguing fixture at Hill Dickinson Stadium between Everton and Chelsea.

Everton v Chelsea (12.30pm BST) Brentford v Liverpool (3pm BST) Fulham v Hull City (3pm BST) Manchester City v Ipswich (3pm BST) Newcastle v Aston Villa (5.30pm BST)

Tom will be here shortly on what promises to be another lively day in the Premier League and beyond. In the meantime, here is Barney Ronay’s column on … the former Crystal Palace chair’s rage in the age of the algorithm constantly churning.

Alonso is also dealing with the absence of Reece James for three months after the defender underwent knee surgery after picking up an injury in training. In the absence of his captain, Alonso is determined to build on Chelsea’s strong display in 5-1 win over Bournemouth last weekend at the Hill Dickinson against Everton.

“You need a lot of clean sheets to win trophies,” he said. “But you [also] need to score a lot of goals. So it’s about being strong in defence, being good in attack and we are in that process. “The obsession is to win and to compete in the best possible way. The clean sheets will come, I’m pretty sure of that, because we want to play with good balance and good control.”
Meanwhile David Moyes believes Jordan Pickford will relish the challenge to his England place from James Trafford and remains the nation’s undisputed No 1 goalkeeper.

Pickford and Trafford shared goalkeeping duties during the recent four-game international break as part of an arranged plan by manager Thomas Tuchel. The 24-year-old Leeds player is considered the biggest threat to emerge to Pickford’s long-held position with the national team but Moyes insists the Everton keeper has been sharper than ever this season.

“When Jordan came back from the World Cup, it might be the best I have ever seen him,” the Everton manager said. “He was lean, he was sharp, his footwork was brilliant, he was fast across the goal and if you look at some of the saves he has made between now and then he has made a couple of brilliant, brilliant saves.

He’s a big-hearted little clown; I’m so glad he’s my son.” When he showed the children, “Janka immediately asked me to take the same shot of her, which often happens. Lóci said it looked like he was among mountains, or as though a monster was about to eat him.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
The photographer was holidaying with his family when two shadows became a plaything for his young son

G ellért Gombai, his wife and two children spend much of the year at their home in Budapest, Hungary, but most of their summers in Alsóörs. “It’s a small holiday village on Lake Balaton, the largest in central Europe, so it’s often referred to as the Hungarian sea,” Gombai, a freelance photographer, says. “We go to the playground and beach most days, swim, and eat beach food, but even when I’m enjoying my holiday, I’m looking out for interesting moments to capture.”

On this particular day, the family had eaten hotdogs for lunch, before Gombai had taken the kids, Lóci and Janka, to the playground. “Lóci, who was five at the time, was jumping between two shadows – one from a changing room, and the other from a building’s roof,” he says. “I asked him to stay still for a few minutes while I got the shot, and he lay like this on the ground. He’s a big-hearted little clown; I’m so glad he’s my son.” When he showed the children, “Janka immediately asked me to take the same shot of her, which often happens. Lóci said it looked like he was among mountains, or as though a monster was about to eat him.”

Gombai applied his phone’s “dramatic cool” filter, and made some minor adjustments. “I really liked the slightly metaphysical spaces created by light and shadow,” he says. “If I forget for a moment it’s my son, I see a carefree form lying in the light while the darkness has bitten a large piece out of the space. Even still, it doesn’t feel sad to me. I have the feeling that the light is pushing the darkness apart.”

articles.content:
The former British Vogue editor-in-chief and author on a romantic kiss on a traffic island, her school-run regrets, and a very expensive nude

B orn in London, Alexandra Shulman, 68, studied social anthropology at the University of Sussex. She was a secretary at Over 21 magazine and, in the early 80s, became a journalist at Tatler. In 1990, she was made editor of British GQ and, from 1992 to 2017, she was editor‑in‑chief of British Vogue. For her contribution to fashion journalism, she was awarded both an OBE and a CBE. Her books include novels and the bestselling memoir, Clothes … and Other Things That Matter. A collection of essays, Black Coffee and Red Lipstick: Notes on Living , is out now. She is married for the second time, has a son and lives in London.

When were you happiest? Anytime that I’m lying in the sun next to a swimming pool with a good book.

Which living person do you most admire, and why? The king, for the amount of work he’s doing while going through cancer treatment.

Aside from property, what’s the most expensive thing you’ve bought? A Roger Hilton gouache of a nude.

What would your superpower be? To teleport myself to places so I didn’t have to go on a plane.

If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose? A human voice on the phone.

What is your most unappealing habit? Not closing cupboards and drawers.

Which book are you ashamed not to have read? Literally the whole canon of classic English literature.

What is your guiltiest pleasure? Drinking a bottle of wine while binge‑watching something for hours.

What was the best kiss of your life? A kiss on a traffic island in Paddington – I was 28.

If you could edit your past, what would you change? I wish I’d been able to pick my son up more often from school. When I see parents at the school gates now it nearly makes me cry.

What single thing would improve the quality of your life? Having a more sunny disposition.

What is the most important lesson life has taught you? That, basically, if a thing’s worth doing, it’s worth doing any old how. Perfection is the enemy of achievement.

articles.content:
How will Brentford and Liverpool fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options

Brentford are flying high in the Premier League as one of just three teams still to suffer defeat this season, although Keith Andrews surely wants his team to convert some of their draws into wins.

Liverpool, on the other hand, return to league action after last weekend’s humbling home defeat to Manchester City. Andoni Iraola’s side responded by putting six goals past Lask in the Champions League, but the Reds are lacking balance.

The last five meetings between Brentford and Liverpool at the Gtech Community Stadium have produced no fewer than 22 goals. The recent goalscoring form of both sides suggests the pattern could continue.

Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Premier League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.

Only Arsenal and Manchester City have claimed more points at home than Brentford this season. Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur have both been stung badly by the Bees whose threat in transition and potency from set pieces will be a problem for Liverpool this weekend.

Defensively, Liverpool remain as vulnerable as they were under Arne Slot last season. Iraola has struggled to find the right formula in the centre of the pitch with Hugo Ekitike, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all expected to miss Saturday’s game through injury. Ryan Gravenberch is also unavailable through suspension.

Liverpool have conceded six goals in their last two games. Brentford will take encouragement from this, as well as the fact they won their last home meeting with the Merseyside outfit last October. This promises to be a compelling clash.

Player to watch: Bradley Barcola, Liverpool - The French winger scored a hat-trick in Liverpool’s mid-week win over LASK, highlighting how the €125m summer signing is bedding in. Barcola will be a threat down the left side and in behind the Brentford backline.

articles.title: The ESPN producer who quit over gambling – and the stories she says went untold
articles.summary: Nicole Noren says ESPN sidelined investigations into sports betting companies as gambling partnerships reshaped the network’s priorities Earlier this week, investigative journalist Nicole Noren did something almost impossible for someone who has spent her career behind the scenes. She made herself the story. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Nicole Noren says ESPN sidelined investigations into sports betting companies as gambling partnerships reshaped the network’s priorities

Earlier this week, investigative journalist Nicole Noren did something almost impossible for someone who has spent her career behind the scenes.

The longtime producer for ESPN’s Outside the Lines used her own experience to shed light on the way sports betting partnerships are warping sports media coverage. The issue wasn’t how ESPN was covering sports gambling, but that it was doing so less and less.

Noren was used to pitching hard-hitting stories around leagues, owners and athletes. As a producer for the investigative reporting arm of the sports network, her team had traditionally been insulated from the business concerns at ESPN , but she started to notice a change about seven years ago.

“What was telling to me was that I had pitched numerous stories that would take a harder look at some of the gambling companies and addiction, and none of those stories was greenlit,” Noren told the Columbia Journalism Review in an interview with journalist Danny Funt. “They ended up doing a show on it around that time, but it became very neutered. Some of the people involved intended to make it much more hard-hitting and hold the gambling companies accountable. Let’s just say the final product didn’t end up doing that.”

Noren, who detailed a family history that included seeing her grandfather, father and brother’s lives unspool due to gambling addiction, left the network in 2023 after ESPN announced the debut of ESPN BET, a partnership with Penn Entertainment.

“I’m not going to work for a gambling company and have blood on my hands,” Noren bluntly told Funt.

ESPN released a statement in response: “ESPN remains committed to journalism that serves sports fans, holds powerful interests accountable and earns our audience’s trust. Our editorial decisions are guided by news judgment and journalistic integrity, and we demonstrate this every day through the award-winning content we produce across our platforms .”

Before he retired in 2019, Bob Ley was the venerable face of Outside the Lines, which included a daily network show with deeply reported TV packages and roundtable discussions on the biggest issues in sports. (Full disclosure: I was a contributor to that show from 2010 to 2017 while working at ESPN.)

“The greatest luxury in television is time and investigative reporting is the feature of a mature news organization,” said Ley, one of the most respected anchors in sports. “It’s not just the box score, it’s the financial pages and the police report.”

He describes Noren as “passionate, honest and indefatigable”. During his tenure at the Worldwide Leader, Ley said, reporters had the leeway to cover entities that had a business relationship with ESPN. If that meant uncovering something unsavory, reporters would have editorial support and ask the subjects of those stories for comment. Sometimes, Ley said, the access even improved those stories.

The network canceled Outside the Lines as a regular show in 2023, although some content is still produced under the brand. A former reporter at the network, who didn’t want to be named since they still work in media, said that the brand is obviously pulling back from investigative journalism, although there are still excellent journalists producing quality work, as ESPN pivots toward entertainment.

Meanwhile Mike Foss , an ESPN executive vice-president, told a conference last week that popular sports personality Pat McAfee “might be a journalist at heart”. “This is a dam-breaking moment,” said Brian Moritz, an associate professor at the Jandoli School of Communication at St Bonaventure University. “What stood out to me: everything that people assumed was happening around sports media is actually happening. To have a former producer at ESPN say it is eye-opening.”

In 2018, the US supreme court overturned the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, allowing states to regulate sports betting markets within their boundaries. Since then, 39 states and Washington DC have established some form of sports betting , although there is wide variation in what is allowed state-to-state. Last April, St Bonaventure and Siena College released the results of a poll showing that 27% of Americans and 52% of men ages 18 to 49 now have an account with a sportsbook.

That’s the same demographic traditionally associated with sports viewership.

“ESPN makes a lot of money from promoting sports gambling,” Moritz said. “And there’s interest in it – a lot of young men want to gamble. But that really makes you ask, what is the mission of ESPN?”

Moritz noted that the rise in sports betting isn’t without cost to those consumers. According to the National Council on Problem Gambling, there has not been a nationwide survey on how addictive sports betting is since the activity became more widely legalized, but the NCPG cited research in recent congressional testimony showing New Jersey, Ohio and Indiana have experienced a rise in problem gambling that tracks with adoption.

“The young, male population that engages in sports fan activity is a Venn diagram with the demographic at risk for a gambling problem,” said Cait Huble, director of public affairs for the NCPG, which is a nonpartisan organization that advocates for harm reduction.

The group is lobbying for the Points Act, which would require a percentage of the federal excise tax on sports bets to be allocated back to the states for prevention, treatment and research into of problem betting.

“What troubles me most is the disconnect at the ESPN executive level between making money and caring about the human impact of constantly bombarding fans with betting odds and talk,” Noren said. “It’s become impossible to escape.”

DraftKings has been ESPN’s official sportsbook and odds provider since 2025. The press release announcing the partnership said the content would be “integrated across ESPN’s ecosystem”. Many ESPN shows and live broadcasts now contain features on betting strategy and updated odds.

“Game coverage is now framed by betting coverage,” said Ley, who now spends his time working with the Seton Hall Center for Sports Media, which he founded. “It’s bigger than just sports, the whole media landscape is being overturned. Even companies as big as ESPN are facing substantial pressures and having to change their business models.”

Being a vocal opponent of a revenue stream is not a route to job security. The Pew Research Center, utilizing Bureau of Labor Statistics data, reported that newsroom jobs declined by 26% between 2008 and 2020. Even the industry giants aren’t immune. The Washington Post, one of the few outlets where sports reporters were still critically covering the betting industry, eliminated its sports department in February.

ESPN has had regular and wide-reaching layoffs every two years or so for the last decade.

“I empathize with people who work at large media companies,” Noren said in the Q&A. “It’s really risky in this landscape to speak out.”

It may seem almost impossible to curtail sports betting’s pull on the sports media landscape given the current White House’s disinterest in regulating business. Congress has made the Protect College Sports Act the legislative priority in the sports space, meaning sports betting and sports prediction markets seem to be on the back burner.

Even if regulation is on the horizon, journalists are under a more immediate constraint: working in an industry that relies on sports betting for a good part of the operating budget.

“These jobs are hard to come by especially if you are younger,” said Moritz, referencing in particular the students he teaches who want to make a name in this industry. “Do you even feel like you can take a stand?”

During his tenure at the Worldwide Leader, Ley said, reporters had the leeway to cover entities that had a business relationship with ESPN. If that meant uncovering something unsavory, reporters would have editorial support and ask the subjects of those stories for comment. Sometimes, Ley said, the access even improved those stories.

The network canceled Outside the Lines as a regular show in 2023, although some content is still produced under the brand. A former reporter at the network, who didn’t want to be named since they still work in media, said that the brand is obviously pulling back from investigative journalism, although there are still excellent journalists producing quality work, as ESPN pivots toward entertainment.

Meanwhile Mike Foss , an ESPN executive vice-president, told a conference last week that popular sports personality Pat McAfee “might be a journalist at heart”. “This is a dam-breaking moment,” said Brian Moritz, an associate professor at the Jandoli School of Communication at St Bonaventure University. “What stood out to me: everything that people assumed was happening around sports media is actually happening. To have a former producer at ESPN say it is eye-opening.”

In 2018, the US supreme court overturned the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, allowing states to regulate sports betting markets within their boundaries. Since then, 39 states and Washington DC have established some form of sports betting , although there is wide variation in what is allowed state-to-state. Last April, St Bonaventure and Siena College released the results of a poll showing that 27% of Americans and 52% of men ages 18 to 49 now have an account with a sportsbook.
That’s the same demographic traditionally associated with sports viewership.
“ESPN makes a lot of money from promoting sports gambling,” Moritz said. “And there’s interest in it – a lot of young men want to gamble. But that really makes you ask, what is the mission of ESPN?”

Moritz noted that the rise in sports betting isn’t without cost to those consumers. According to the National Council on Problem Gambling, there has not been a nationwide survey on how addictive sports betting is since the activity became more widely legalized, but the NCPG cited research in recent congressional testimony showing New Jersey, Ohio and Indiana have experienced a rise in problem gambling that tracks with adoption.

“The young, male population that engages in sports fan activity is a Venn diagram with the demographic at risk for a gambling problem,” said Cait Huble, director of public affairs for the NCPG, which is a nonpartisan organization that advocates for harm reduction.

The group is lobbying for the Points Act, which would require a percentage of the federal excise tax on sports bets to be allocated back to the states for prevention, treatment and research into of problem betting.

“What troubles me most is the disconnect at the ESPN executive level between making money and caring about the human impact of constantly bombarding fans with betting odds and talk,” Noren said. “It’s become impossible to escape.”

DraftKings has been ESPN’s official sportsbook and odds provider since 2025. The press release announcing the partnership said the content would be “integrated across ESPN’s ecosystem”. Many ESPN shows and live broadcasts now contain features on betting strategy and updated odds.

“Game coverage is now framed by betting coverage,” said Ley, who now spends his time working with the Seton Hall Center for Sports Media, which he founded. “It’s bigger than just sports, the whole media landscape is being overturned. Even companies as big as ESPN are facing substantial pressures and having to change their business models.”

Being a vocal opponent of a revenue stream is not a route to job security. The Pew Research Center, utilizing Bureau of Labor Statistics data, reported that newsroom jobs declined by 26% between 2008 and 2020. Even the industry giants aren’t immune. The Washington Post, one of the few outlets where sports reporters were still critically covering the betting industry, eliminated its sports department in February.
ESPN has had regular and wide-reaching layoffs every two years or so for the last decade.
“I empathize with people who work at large media companies,” Noren said in the Q&A. “It’s really risky in this landscape to speak out.”

It may seem almost impossible to curtail sports betting’s pull on the sports media landscape given the current White House’s disinterest in regulating business. Congress has made the Protect College Sports Act the legislative priority in the sports space, meaning sports betting and sports prediction markets seem to be on the back burner.
Even if regulation is on the horizon, journalists are under a more immediate constraint: working in an industry that relies on sports betting for a good part of the operating budget.

“These jobs are hard to come by especially if you are younger,” said Moritz, referencing in particular the students he teaches who want to make a name in this industry. “Do you even feel like you can take a stand?”

articles.title: Australia 21-43 New Zealand: Bledisloe Cup rugby union international – as it happened
articles.summary: All Blacks secure 13th straight win against Wallabies Barrett and Moorby score two tries each at Accor Stadium It’s skipper Codie Taylor that is out onto the field first though, leading his players past Nathan Charles, allowing every All Black to shake the former Wallaby hooker by the hand. Damien McKenzie is responsible for the final prematch rev-up. Vision of his address appears to show every member of the New Zealand squad wearing bright coral pink boots to sign off their otherwise entirely black outfit. It’s a very strong look. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Thank you for joining me this afternoon. That concludes our winter and spring international rugby season on this particular page. I’ll leave you with Jack Snape’s on-the-whistle match report form Accor Stadium, and bid you farewell.

The Wallabies lived up to pre-match fears that an increasingly threadbare squad had reached breaking point. Only Max Jorgensen emerged with any great credit from a performance that lacked cohesion in both attack and defence. Isaac Henry, Harry Potter and Declan Meredith all had their moments, but they also indicated they are not the players capable of beating the All Blacks on a dry track when both teams are committed to running the ball.

For the half an hour before the interval there was a real lack of leadership and presence in gold, which Les Kiss will be keen to fix before next year’s world cup.

In the first half, when the game was live, the All Blacks were imperious. Their back row monstered the Wallabies, setting up quick ball for McKenzie to have a day out with. For the second week running he was excellent, feeding his runners with precision, keeping the defensive line on the move, and pulling the correct rein when a score was in sight. Beauden Barrett remains top class, Josh Moorby was excellent, and Rieko Ioane coming off the bench is the very definition of strength in depth. Their 37 points to half-time flattered Australia.

“I’m surrounded by a great bunch of men who make my job easy,” purrs Cody Taylor.

“Not good enough,” admits Harry Wilson. “We’ve got to start better, we can’t get that far behind the All Blacks.”

He credits the effort late on but bemoans it as “too little too late.”

The second half of that contest will not live long in the memory. Credit to Australia for digging in, but this afternoon was all about that scintillating first-40 effort from the All Blacks.

The All Blacks extend their winning streak over the Wallabies to 13 matches. It’s a run that doesn’t look like ending any time soon.

79 mins: The 13-man All Blacks slow the game down, milk the phases, and run down the clock.

78 mins: Despite playing against just 13 men the Wallabies lack the direction to engineer space. It’s little surprise when the ball goes to ground after Henry tried to feed Canham through a keyhole.

77 mins: Australia get to work in attacking territory, but it’s slow disconnected phase play.

Suaalii stood up Fihaki one on one on the left wing. The debutant executed the tackle, but he didn’t get particularly low, so when the two men clashed heads it left the TMO and on-field referee little room to manoeuvre. The All Blacks will see off the game with just 13 players.

76 mins: There’s another long TMO intervention, this time scrutinising an All Black tackle that could have collected Suaalii in the head.

75 mins: It’s not crisp but it is effective as offloads and hopeful passes keep finding their targets before McLaughlin-Phillips makes another impressive dash – but he loses in contact on the ground and the All Blacks can take a breather.

74 mins: The All Blacks put their heads down and bums up inside their own half to grind the game down. Then the bomb goes up, it’s contested and Australia are forced to scramble near their 22. Harry McLaughlin-Phillips does well with his first carry as the Wallabies resume their last ditch efforts.

72 mins : Another shonky All Black lineout, this time picked off by Williams. Daugunu reaches halfway on the counter on the right before the ball goes through hands to the left. Australia are desperate to run deep lines but New Zealand’s defence is up too quickly to shut down any space. The Wallabies are determined to keep the ball alive at all costs and that makes for some funky passes, and clunky bobbles. Jorgensen almost pierces the line on the right, then Meredith through the middle, the latter supported by Wilson, who is stopped in his tracks and play returns to an earlier advantage.

71 mins: 14-man New Zealand take their time in possession, milking the clock, and they’re gifted a penalty by Daugunu who ignores the instructions of the referee to continue playing on the ground when warned not to.

70 mins: Can Australia inject some life into things? That’s a hard no. From behind the scrum Meredith engages the line then misses his burst runner.

69 mins: Awful lineout fumble on a short throw by the All Blacks. The tension in this contest has evaporated into the western Sydney sky. This is typified by New Zealand being forced to play with just 14 after spending all their replacements.

… and that desperation is rewarded handsomely! Wright takes a cheeky short drop-out that catches New Zealand unawares. Suddenly there are gold jerseys flooding forward at speed with the All Blacks miles out of position. Daugunu almost scores on the initial play, but he won’t be denied on the second phase. This has been a commendable effort from Australia in the past 20 minutes.

66 mins: The lineout is solid, the maul forms, and from it Taukei’aho shears off like a ricocheting bullet, but as he crosses the line there are three gold jerseys holding him up! Superb desperation from the Australian defenders.

65 mins: New Zealand are awarded an offside penalty near halfway that invites them to kick towards the left corner.

Play has now been recalled all the way back to Meredith’s near-try by the TMO! This is a crazy intervention, miles after the incident. He thinks Roigard committed foul play by kicking the ball out of Meredith’s hands in the act of scoring the try. He clearly didn’t. Thankfully Luke Pearce is on top of it all, handles the situation superbly, and communicates calmly to both skippers. Magnificent on-field refereeing, awful intervention by the TMO.

64 mins: Australia come again from halfway. Suaalii sets it up with an ambitious looping pass. Jorgensen toes ahead and regathers. Then he kicks again, but he’s tackled in the process so there’s no gold jersey to chase the black defenders. In broken field New Zealand counter and Roigard is suddenly so far ahead of his colleagues in space he practically stops to invite support runners to join him. They come on the left and two passes later it’s B Barrett v Meredith on the left wing one-on-one. Barrett kicks ahead – but Meredith wins the chase, then does enough on the ground to avoid conceding the penalty! Brilliant defence from the No 10 just seconds after he was denied a try.

62 mins: Australia get another opportunity to run out of their 22 behind a scrum. Daugunu hits the line hard, Bell supports quickly, Canham is effective, then Meredith is through! He only has Moorby to beat! He jinks one way, then the other, the try line approaching, he’s scragged, but his momentum carries him over the line – then as he reaches out to touch down the pill is knocked from his grasp! Agonising for the No 10.

60 mins: Another Australian attack comes to nought before it has chance to bed in. The TV coverage has shown Wright’s anguished face repeatedly today with the fullback failing to dovetail with his outside back colleagues coming out of defence

Meanwhile, behind play, Shannon Frizell goes down with nobody near him. The big forward hasn’t been on long but his day might already be done with some kind of leg injury.

57 mins: Finally some momentum for the hosts. Canham is powerful up the guts, McReight is busy, and halfway is breached with gusto. But then it all falls apart as the New Zealand defence rushes up with menace, forcing ball carriers backwards. Daugunu finds himself in quicksand, as does De Lutiis and a promising move ebbs away. The eventual kick down the right channel is allowed to bobble out of play. Australia infringe at the lineout and the visitors kick clear.

Wilson picks up the ball behind an unconvincing scrum and Australia lose territory as their midfield stalls. Finally Jorgensen injects some magic with a jinking run down the right to set up front foot ball on the 22. Finally the backs connect: Meredith to Suaalii, to Potter – who is hauled down inches short, but Wright follows up and dives over in the corner. After a long period on the back foot, finally something for Sydneysiders to celebrate. That was all about the excellence of Max Jorgensen on the right wing.

Lonergan slots over a very good conversion to provide another reason to cheer.

53 mins : Sititi smashes another chink in the gold armour allowing Fihaki to canter into open field. Inexplicably he leaves the ball behind attempting to grubber on the 22 and Australia can counter. Lonergan runs the ball the other way but there’s no connection and both teams have a little breather. The edge has gone out of this contest somewhat. It’s now just a matter of how many points the All Blacks can pour on if they remain disciplined enough.

52 mins: Wilson taps and runs from halfway but gets flattened. The ball comes out slowly to the left but there’s a handling. The Wallabies look absolutely shot. They look a full weight division outmatched here.

50 mins: New Zealand feed a scrum on the 22. Lakai drills his way into the gold line, Moorby follows up, but he can’t recycle and Lonergan and Tizzano complete a well-executed turnover.

47 mins: New Zealand grind their way through the phases in their own half. Tavatavanawai puts a dint in the line on the right, allowing McKenzie to showcase his quick hands on the inside and set runners away on the left. Play stalls by the 22 but phases 12 and 13 are solid with S Barrett and Sititi throwing their weight around. Finally, about three minutes into the drive, there’s a loose pass to the left and the attack finally runs out of road. That might be the first time New Zealand have mounted a purposeful attack without scoring all match.

44 mins: The All Blacks have been irresistible going forward but Australia’s defence has been abject. They are staring down back-to-back 50-point shellackings.

Williams is back on the field and he wins lineout ball near halfway. Henry is strong to accept contact, then Bell shoves his way over the gainline. It’s slow from the Wallabies as New Zealand force them backwards and it’s no surprise when an errant pass from behind the ruck lands in front of Salakaia-Loto and the All Blacks counter at pace! Lakai is devastating on the burst into broken field. McKenzie enforces the squeeze with a kick in behind that’s recovered his side’s way. As phases build Moorby threads the eye of a needle on the left wing, dummying dramatically, then slipping along the touchline and in at the corner.

The All Blacks are very very good with ball in hand. Australia are being reminded of their place in the international rugby pecking order.

Australia claim the dropout and mount another siege. With the half-time siren approaching they cut to the right, but it’s all bit slow and too close to the defensive line. Suaalii offloads under pressure high to Jorgensen, who attempts to keep the ball moving, but his next move is telegraphed, Beauden Barrett reads it, plucks the simple interception, then runs 90m virtually unopposed to rubber stamp his team’s dominance.

39 mins: The lineout is solid, the maul forms, but it’s undermanned and the All Blacks hold it up. Australia head infield with Wilson and Nasser shoving the gainline inches forward. McReight picks the ball off the floor of the ruck and launches himself over bodies like an NFL running back on fourth and one – but he’s held up and New Zealand survive.

38 mins: The All Blacks concede an offside penalty in possession allowing Australia to kick to the right corner. Can they capitalise?

37 mins: Australia secure lineout ball and invite Valetini to bulldoze into the black wall. The Wallabies recycle but quickly run out of room on the right with Potter throwing an errant pass.

36 mins: From the halfway scrum New Zealand run to the right but lack cohesion and Meredith does well to win the turnover on the ground.

34 mins: Meredith’s short kick-off doesn’t carry 10m. 14-man Australia are drowning, not waving. The All Blacks could run up a cricket score at this rate.

articles.content:
The ruthless All Blacks embarrassed the Wallabies in their final home Test of the year, brushing aside the golden pretenders 43-21 in Sydney, a second thrashing in a week that makes a mockery of the hosts’ ambitions for next year’s World Cup.

The All Blacks were too fast at the breakdown, the ball hardly slowing as the New Zealanders appeared to advance it at will. They spoiled all but three Wallaby attacking forays, aided by errors and execution failures.

Captain Harry Wilson was blunt after the Wallabies’ 13th straight loss against their trans-Tasman rivals. “It’s not good enough for this group, we’ve got to be a lot better,” he told Channel Nine.

“We’ve got to start better. We had a terrible second half in the first game [of the series]. We had a terrible first half this game. We can’t be having terrible halves against the All Blacks. In the second half, we showed a bit of grit, but it’s too late, mate. We can’t be that far behind.”

Two second-half tries by the Wallabies thinned the margin slightly, but could not temper the conclusion obvious to all those who watched. So comprehensive was this defeat, Australia’s standing before next year’s showpiece must now be re-evaluated. From outsiders for the trophy aided by home support, Les Kiss’s side are now utterly irrelevant, likable entertainers at best. Maybe they will provide a good excuse for a party after the victory over Hong Kong in the opener.

The turnaround of the past two weeks is such a disappointment for the longsuffering Australian rugby community after the early promise shown under Kiss. Any momentum has now evaporated and the Wallabies find themselves in reverse.

Kiss was scathing in his assessment of the team’s first half. “There’s got to be a little bit more thinking about what it really means to actually turn up in that first half and make sure we don’t make those errors that we did,” he said. “It’s just not acceptable what was put out there.”

The enduring image of this catastrophe of an afternoon was the second try for All Blacks Josh Moorby, when a feigned overhead pass fooled Max Jorgensen and Ryan Lonergan – two of the most impressive Wallabies in recent months. Stationary in the late afternoon sun, the Australian pair were little more than a guard of honour for the All Blacks winger who crossed untouched.

Much of the speculation among the Australian rugby community before the match was how Declan Meredith would fare . The fly half was responsible for two outstanding moments in the second half, including a near try when put through by impactful substitutes Angus Bell and Josh Canham, and a counterattack from a cheeky Tom Wright short drop-out. But any deep assessment of individuals would be an indulgence after a one-sided shellacking that was over before half-time, even if the contest showed promise in its early stages.

The All Blacks were forced into a late change when Jordie Barrett pulled out with calf tightness. His absence was amplified when Quinn Tupaea left the field dazed after hitting his head on the turf after just one minute.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, back at 13 after two Tests on the wing, was influential early alongside Wright and Jorgensen, who twice found space down the right. But it was the movement left off a lineout that almost put Australia ahead. The final ball from Jorgensen went to ground when Harry Potter and Wright both had clear space in front of them.

The inability to make the most of early field position was punished when the All Blacks ventured up the other end for the first time. Wright and Potter made try-saving tackles on the left, but when the All Blacks spread it to the openside the golden line was stretched thin and Moorby crossed.

The Wallabies have been profligate in recent weeks with their opportunities, and the theme continued. An attacking lineout was wasted when Fraser McReight dropped the ball as the maul was being formed. Within seconds the field had flipped, and full-back Beauden Barrett finished off a gorgeous midfield break from flanker Peter Lakai, put through by fly half Damian McKenzie.

Within three phases off the restart the All Blacks were back on the Wallabies’ line, their ruck speed like lightning, and in another three Lakai was over for another. A Lonergan box kick drifted too deep, allowing the All Blacks to clear their lines easily, then the hosts lost the ensuing lineout. Within a minute Rieko Ioane was over in the corner and the score was 22-0.

Finally there was something for the home crowd to cheer when Meredith put Jeremy Williams over. His joy was short lived when at the other end a harsh offside call saw him yellow carded. From the base of the scrum Wallace Sititi snuck over to resume normal programming. A Barrett intercept from a Jorgensen pass, punished with a run away try, and the conversion from McKenzie, made it 36-7 at the break.

After Moorby’s sleight of hand and try early in the second period, the Wallabies bench players stemmed the bleeding. Jorgensen, Wright and Harry Potter combined twice down the right to record Australia’s second five-pointer, and Filipo Daugunu scored after Meredith and Wright’s quick thinking. The match petered out, as Harry McLaughlin-Phillips relieved Meredith for his debut.

The Bledisloe Cup whitewash restores some pride after the All Blacks’ 3-1 series defeat to South Africa. Their ability to do it with a long injury list including their captain Ardie Savea, their two top fly halves Ruben Love and Richie Mo’unga, and their influential centre Jordie Barrett, confirms their place as the major challenger to the Springboks at next year’s World Cup. It’s also significant that they secured this victory at Accor Stadium, which will host much of the pointy end of the tournament.

The wayward Wallabies have four Tests in Europe to come in 2026, before the long off-season break. After this performance, few will be looking forward to their first Test of 2027, against the All Blacks again on Anzac Day.

articles.title: Savaged by Simon Jordan – and thanks to the algorithm I want to be savaged again | Barney Ronay

articles.content:
The former Palace chair seeming very angry indeed about others’ opinions is just par for the course as football’s age of rage ramps up another level

Yet again the mainstream wokealorium is preachifying from its pulpitrex. It’s egregious. It’s sanctiforial. It’s a wangitude of complete retardifaction.

This has not been an easy column to write. It has been difficult, gruelling in parts, but also warm, exhilarating and at times deeply erotic. Yes. I was SAVAGED by Simon Jordan. And I’ve never felt so alive.

You know who Simon Jordan is. Used to own Crystal Palace. Now a very good and listenable pundit on TalkSport , where he does the grown-up topics. Simon Jordan has strong opinions. This is his thing. His worldview says: the world is bad. The world is in need of correction. And he’s right about that, as he often is about things.

That’s what makes this all a bit surprising because I like Simon Jordan! I listen to his morning show with Jim White and it’s often really good. I respect the fact he has industry knowledge because he ran a football club. And yes that involved lots of dealings with Steve Bruce, Iain Dowie or similar, but it’s still basically the same thing.

I like the way he pops up in clips looking like an exquisitely powdered 17th-century Umbrian count, some gorgeous little angry blond glove-puppet I want to sit on my knee and pet and cosset and whisper in his ear about granditudinous hypocralism, in a way that’s just warm and fond and not, for me, in any way sexual, but which definitely is for him.

I like the way he talks. It reminds me of Jackie Chiles, the lawyer in Seinfeld, saying it’s outrageous, egregious, preposterous . Sometimes this can have a Mrs Malaprop edge. But that’s also fun and even then you get his point, which is usually good, even if you didn’t expect to agree, or can only agree secretly. When you’re right you’re right. When you’re veritudinously superfactual you’re veritudinously superfactual.

By now you’re probably wondering what happened. Well, I was definitely savaged. No one can take that away from me. And yes this was a week ago, but other stuff happened in between and I forgot about it for a while. I also haven’t fully listened to the savaging. It’s two minutes long and life is short.

In fact I only know about it because my friend and colleague Barry Glendenning is very reliable in this respect. If you’re ever cancelled, owned, or significantly beasted on the internet then Barry will let you know, as an act of love and kindness, and not, repeat not, because he enjoys it and is killing time in the pub on his phone. It’s like having a faithful and attentive online Lassie. What’s that? Slow down boy. Wait, you’re saying Michaela Strachan has called me a nonce? On LinkedIn? Good boy. Easy. There you go. Here’s a lovely bowl of vape oil and Guinness.

I have to admit I am also amplifying this, promoting myself as genuinely savage-worthy. In reality I was savaged in a minor, offhand way that I still don’t really get. I was at Croatia versus England in Rijeka . The game was meant to be played without fans as punishment for some Croatia-related disorder in Paris last year, which included accusations of people making Nazi salutes.

In the event the Croatian FA filled the ground with children, which is allowed under a loophole in the rules. It felt a bit weird in the moment . At the very least it didn’t seem to fit the spirit of the offence. Nazism, yes, bad. But also: a lovely day out for Year 8.

I still don’t really get why anyone would strongly disagree with this. It seems obvious enough. Yeah, everyone likes happy jolly children. Personally I believe the children are our future. I’ve always said that. But they’re not some kind of smart bomb that disintegrates the capacity for logic.

The counter-argument seems to be that this is joyless liberal Guardian stuff. It’s the woke mind-virus. It’s being too interested in not promoting nazism, when you should simply enjoy the laughter of little boys.

And yes Simon Jordan is right. It is annoying to be preached at. But we’re not talking libtard snowflake stuff here. We’re talking actual Nazis, people who just like and enjoy swastikas, who talk fondly about the Ustase, arguably the most vicious sect of the Third Reich war machine. I don’t know, man. The more I hear about the Nazis, the less I like the sound of them.

Plus we now have the sight of Hajduk Split fans this week walking behind an actual coffin and chanting “Auschwitz”. Does this seem like the message is being hammered home? At the very least we’re going to need more children. How many is this one going to take? Ten thousand? Maybe if we can get children to carry a coffin through Amsterdam then it’s fine and just a heartwarming event that shows lessons are being learned.

This is how it goes you see. You are supposed to LASH BACK in these situations. But it’s all a bit weird. Suddenly Simon Jordan is attacking me with children. He’s barging me out of the way in Starbucks with his mega-buggy, one hand clutched to his pearl-draped throat, saying, what about the children, the children, the children?

You see? I’m being sucked in. Because this is what the internet will do to you. I wasn’t even the main savaging that day. I was a side-beef, an afterthought. By now the algorithm is already filling my feed with fresh SJ face-offs, the latest a “heated exchange” with Dale Vince about Robbie Savage, in itself a mouthwatering trio, perpetual savaging motion in action.

In the end this is the only real point of interest here. This stuff is utterly addictive. And with good reason: it’s designed to be. Vast amounts of expertise and resources have been poured into this irresistible machinery. David Squires did a brilliant cartoon this week about the rise of the celebrity football chat-cast , the industrial-scale, seed-funded waffle that must now justify its space by shouting above the noise, and which will always tend towards beef-culture and a narrative of opposition.

I’ve tried really hard to stay out of this. I don’t do radio or TV stuff, because, well, what’s the point, but more because nobody’s clean, nobody escapes, suddenly you’re having a charity boxing grudge-match with Stephen Warnock.

But it is worth logging for the record that we are at fever pitch. The level of rage around football right now is genuinely astonishing. The story of the Manchester City verdict is, in part, a regulatory ruling over a breach of financial rules. But really it’s the astonishing post-truth online response, the urge to assail and objectify and dehumanise over a tribunal’s interpretation of accountancy practices.

Just going to report on a game at the Etihad this week involved BRAVELY DEFYING assorted threats of violence in response to articles written in these pages. And yes, these are clearly the work of a 77-year-old hunchback in Jakarta, or a drunk and bored corporate lawyer taking a break from surfing porn on the family computer.

But it is all part of the design too. This is meant to happen. A new book called Our Minds Under Siege by Bruno Giussani, a former global curator of TED, describes the way algorithm life is actively changing human behaviour . This is not a secret. Marketing has wanted to do this since the early 20th century.

Walter Dill Scott’s Theory of Suggestion. The Drive Theory of Motivation. The deliberate creation of want and anxiety into the way we sell things. And now we have a new and commercially irresistible language. Dopamine craving. Variable social validation. The feedback loop.

The way even random scrolling is controlled and metered, designed to create a craving that’s always there inside your head, and controlled by tech platforms that openly define humans as eyeballs, want, need, hunger.

In the end, this is why Simon Jordan seems to care so violently about someone else’s opinions on the children-washing of Uefa sanctions. It’s why I’m just incredibly excited by this as an outcome, why I want more not less. Savage me again. Make me feel something. Let me exist inside the machine with you, egregious, preposterous, vibramoniously alive.

articles.title: Call for more food funding due to high living cost
articles.summary: Deputy Louise Doublet does not think the cost of living was considered in the ending of a trial.
articles.content:
Deputy Louise Doublet said she thought the cost of living was not taken into consideration in the decision

A Jersey politician said she thought cost-of-living pressures were not considered by the government when it chose to end a trial of free fruit in primary schools.

Since 2024 children in four primary schools have been able to get apples, bananas and other fruit as part of the pilot scheme.

Deputy Louise Doublet said: "To have that taken away at a time when the cost of living is still increasing I think has been quite hard for some families".

The education minister ended the trial because not enough children were eating the fruit and it was leading to a lot of wastage. The Government of Jersey has been approached for a comment.

The government announced in September fresh fruit would be included in a school food programme that provides hot school meals for government primary schools.

Minister for Education and Lifelong Learning Catherine Curtis previously said the free fruit scheme was leading to "a lot of wastage" and parents "actually asked" for fruit to be incorporated into the school food programme instead.

Doublet said the minister had responded to her questions in the assembly "centred around the evidence and she informed the assembly that it hadn't resulted in much of an increase in children actually consuming fruit and vegetables and I do accept that".

But she added she did not think benefits in terms of cost of living were measured by the scheme.

"Personally I would like to see more investment in healthy food especially if it's locally grown food to help families with the cost of living," she said.

When asked about the contract with UK company Apetito Limited to provide hot school meals for government primary schools across Jersey she said it was the "best available option".

paragraphs: Deputy Louise Doublet said she thought the cost of living was not taken into consideration in the decision
A Jersey politician said she thought cost-of-living pressures were not considered by the government when it chose to end a trial of free fruit in primary schools.
Since 2024 children in four primary schools have been able to get apples, bananas and other fruit as part of the pilot scheme.
Deputy Louise Doublet said: "To have that taken away at a time when the cost of living is still increasing I think has been quite hard for some families".
The education minister ended the trial because not enough children were eating the fruit and it was leading to a lot of wastage. The Government of Jersey has been approached for a comment.
The government announced in September fresh fruit would be included in a school food programme that provides hot school meals for government primary schools.

Minister for Education and Lifelong Learning Catherine Curtis previously said the free fruit scheme was leading to "a lot of wastage" and parents "actually asked" for fruit to be incorporated into the school food programme instead.

Doublet said the minister had responded to her questions in the assembly "centred around the evidence and she informed the assembly that it hadn't resulted in much of an increase in children actually consuming fruit and vegetables and I do accept that".
But she added she did not think benefits in terms of cost of living were measured by the scheme.
"Personally I would like to see more investment in healthy food especially if it's locally grown food to help families with the cost of living," she said.
When asked about the contract with UK company Apetito Limited to provide hot school meals for government primary schools across Jersey she said it was the "best available option".
She added she understood people's concerns around the freshness of the food but her "understanding is that the meals are actually frozen rather than artificially preserved".
"I would like to see these funded meals extended further because it hits the cost of living for parents and... provides healthy meals for children," she said.

articles.title: Avian flu and costs among reasons for loss of captive birds at Castle Espie
articles.summary: Difficulties in transporting animals since Brexit has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds.
articles.content:
Avian flu, cost-cutting and Brexit are among the reasons behind the transfer of captive birds from one of Northern Ireland's best-known wildlife sites, according to the charity that runs it.

Director of Operations at Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) Alex Lane said avian influenza, as well as difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit, has contributed to the decline in the number of captive birds at Castle Espie.

The closure of both the site's captive bird programme and guided school tour programme is part of wider WWT cost-cutting measures.

An Assembly member has described the changes to the education offering as "disappointing".

Alex Lane said the site used to have around 500 birds in its captive collection - but, a combination of Brexit and avian influenza means today, there are fewer than 100.

Both the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs and the UK's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs have been contacted for comment.

From November onwards, all captive birds at Castle Espie will be transferred to other WWT sites across the UK.

The centre, which is located in County Down, will also no longer offer guided school tours.

However, the centre have said they will "continue to welcome self-guided school visits".

Castle Espie, which is managed by the WWT, is located on the shores of Strangford Lough, just outside Comber.

The reserve is a safe haven for native and exotic birds, ducks and geese, and some of its collection including globally at-risk species.

It has different types of wetlands, including freshwater and sailing lagoons as well as seasonally flooded areas.

Cara Hunter said the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing"

SDLP MLA Cara Hunter, who sits on the Stormont education committee, told BBC News NI that the "loss of guided educational visits is disappointing".

"Castle Espie has played an important role in introducing generations of young people to nature, conservation and the unique environment on their doorstep.

"I would be concerned that these changes could reduce opportunities for schools, particularly those with limited resources, to access high-quality environmental education."

The MLA added that "opportunities that educate, inspire and broaden horizons are quietly lost while Stormont remains distracted from the issues that matter most to families".

Alex Lane, Director of Operations at WWT, said rising costs and the challenge around income means charities like the WWT are facing "increasing pressure".

"We've got a sizeable deficit and obviously that's unsustainable in the long term," she told BBC News NI.

Lane said it is important the WWT have surplus income so that they can "do the conservation work that is part of their mission".

She said the site used to have over 500 birds in its captive collection - but, in part due to avian influenza, today there are less than 100.

Lane added that another factor in the decline in the number of captive birds is the increased difficulties in transporting birds since Brexit.

"There is no aligned system for bringing birds into Ireland from mainland UK.

"We've got a vastly reduced collection, and that's not by choice. That is the impact of avian influenza and the restrictions placed on bird movement as a result of Brexit."

It is thought that diverging post-Brexit bio-security checks has increased red tape for moving birds between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

Under the strict mandates of the Windsor Framework, these regulatory shifts also mean heavy administrative and logistical costs.

According to the UK Government's official website , external , the movement of captive birds from Britain to Northern Ireland requires an export health certificate.

There is also a requirement for captive birds to be checked at the point of entry when transported to Northern Ireland, to protect animal health and welfare and public health.

However, Lane said there will be benefits to the decommissioning of the captive bird collection.

"The intent with the site is to reset it as this hub for wetland nature conservation.

Lane said the site "needs to stop" its formal education offering in part due to financial pressures WWT faces.

She added that there is also an insufficient number of schools booking guided tours at the site to cover costs.

Lane said the low number of school visits may be partly be caused by the cost of transport.

articles.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts
articles.summary: Poach your leeks to perfection, then pair with pickled pears and nutty miso I have a great respect for the leek, which is possibly the most demanding vegetable in its need to be freshly cooked before consumption. articles.content:
Poach your leeks to perfection, then pair with pickled pears and nutty miso

I have a great respect for the leek, which is possibly the most demanding vegetable in its need to be freshly cooked before consumption. A warm leek, fresh from the pot, is an ethereal, collapsing sigh of diaphanous veils, whereas cold it can all too easily become a slippery and almost slimy mess of hopelessness.

All the various elements can be made ahead of time except the leeks, which should be just warm from their poaching, and the dressing, which should be made at the last minute. Vegetable bouillon may seem a bit of a faff to make just to poach some leeks (if you prefer, simply cook them in two litres of seasoned water with a dash of white wine instead), but a good, light vegetable broth is a useful thing to have around, and a batch will keep happily in the fridge for three or four days. To toast nuts successfully, cook them on a tray in an even layer in a 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½ oven for 15-20 minutes, which will toast them evenly to the core without scorching.

For the hazelnut miso 250g hazelnuts 40g white miso paste 25 ml olive oil 5g flaky sea salt (about 1 tsp)

For the vegetable bouillon (optional; see recipe introduction) 1 medium carrot , peeled and quartered 1 medium onion , peeled and quartered 1 medium shallot , peeled and left whole 2 garlic cloves , peeled 4 leek tops (from trimming the leeks below) 1 bay leaf 5 thyme sprigs 2 parsley sprigs 1 star anise 150 ml white wine 2 litres filtered water 40g flaky sea salt

For the pickled pears 2 conference pears 150 ml white-wine vinegar 50g sugar

For the leeks 4 leeks , trimmed, roots removed and thoroughly cleaned, then cut in half across the middle 2 litres vegetable boui llon (see above and method) Minced chives and chopped chervil , to finish (optional)

For the dressing 200g pear pickling liquor (see above and method) 100 ml extra-virgin olive oil 5g flaky sea salt (about 1 tsp) 2g ground black pepper (about ½ tsp) 50g minced shallot 10g minced garlic 100g toasted hazelnuts , chopped

The day before, put the nuts in a container or bowl, add a litre of water and leave overnight to soften. Next day, strain the nuts, reserving the soaking liquid.

Put all the bouillon ingredients in a large pot (again, you can do this a day before), bring to a low simmer and cook gently on a medium heat for 25 minutes. Take off the heat, leave to rest and cool for four hours, then strain.

Peel, quarter and core the pears, then cut each quarter in half lengthways and put in a container, for which you have a lid. Put the vinegar, sugar and 75ml water in a saucepan, bring to a simmer, then pour the pickling liquor over the pears, cover and chill for 12 hours.

Put the drained nuts, miso, olive oil and salt in a food processor, dribble in just enough of the soaking liquid to lubricate, then blitz to a smooth, rich puree the consistency of mayonnaise; add a drop more liquid to loosen, if need be.

Submerge the leeks in the bouillon, bring it to a low simmer and cook for 15 minutes, until the leeks show only gentle resistance to the tip of a sharp knife. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature for about half an hour.

Meanwhile, make the dressing. In a stainless-steel bowl, whisk the pickling liquor and oil to a smooth and coherent emulsion, then stir in all the other dressing ingredients.

Lift the just-warm leeks out of the poaching liquid and cut lengthways into quarters. Spoon some hazelnut miso on each plate, then arrange the leeks on top. Dot pieces of pickled pear between them, spoon over the dressing and garnish with minced chives and, if you’re lucky enough to have some, chopped chervil.

Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London
