Brando made it OK for a man to be a sex object.

Many of the actor’s performances eschewed the buttoned-up vision of masculinity in the films of the 1930s and 1940s. He was emotional, violent and physical. “I’d never seen anything as visceral,” wrote the critic Pauline Kael, remembering her first glimpse of Brando on stage in the late 1940s. FB

“Great success here,” wrote Oscar Wilde of the American speaking tour on which this photograph was taken. “Nothing like it since Dickens, they tell me.” Though the 27-year-old had not yet written famous works such as The Importance of Being Earnest and The Picture of Dorian Gray, he was already a society sensation. His tightly controlled performance of a queer, urbane form of masculinity made him famous, but came with great risks. He was later imprisoned for gross indecency with men, and polite society turned on him – perhaps prefigured by newspaper digs at the time about the “effeminate” figure in this portrait. FB

You may not recognise him now, but Sessue Hayakawa was one of Hollywood’s first heart-throbs. Born in Japan, he moved to the US in early adulthood and broke out as a major matinée idol with a star-making turn as the villainous lead in Cecil B DeMille’s The Cheat (1915). He was then one of LA’s highest-paid actors. One photographer recalled Hayakawa arriving at a premiere to a horde of female fans who “spread their fur coats at his feet” so he could avoid stepping in a puddle.

As an Asian leading man, Hayakawa had to put up with a lot of racialised typecasting, and anti-miscegenation laws meant his characters never got the girl; when anti-Japanese sentiment rose in the 1920s, his star faded. He did get a late-career comeback, however, with his Oscar-nominated role as the tyrannical Colonel Saito in 1957’s The Bridge on the River Kwai. GS

Nuba mountain communities in the Kordofan region of Sudan have faced violence from outsiders for centuries, from British colonial authorities to the Khartoum central government. Against this backdrop, a renowned tradition of wrestling tournaments has developed.

This image by Magnum co-founder George Rodger, of a wrestler hoisted on a supporter’s shoulders, brought global, and unwelcome, attention to the area. Former Nazi photographer Leni Riefenstahl produced controversial and exoticising work there. “When they found out what was going on, people felt exploited,” said Sudanese professor Guma Kunda Komey. FB

It’s estimated that around one in four women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence by a male partner. Since the early 1980s, the photojournalist Donna Ferrato has dedicated her career to documenting the devastating impacts of these relationships.

This photo is from Ferrato’s 1991 book Living With the Enemy, which includes texts based on conversations with victims and perpetrators. Over the course of the project, she spent time in women’s shelters as well as riding in police cars and staying in people’s homes. Here, an eight-year-old boy, Diamond, shouts at his father as he is being arrested at their home in Minneapolis: “I hate you for hitting my mother.”

“I’d never seen a child stand up to his abusive father,” Ferrato later recalled . “That blew my mind. The mom hadn’t called the cops – the boy called the cops. He had just shown the police where his father had hidden the screwdriver.” GS

“The most masculine president in the American memory,” according to one recent biographer of Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt. He is pictured here on horseback when he was a lieutenant colonel in an army unit known as the Rough Riders.

His carefully crafted butch image was, on closer inspection, a jumble of contradictions. Raised in extreme wealth, he was fond of being photographed in suspiciously pristine working-class clothing. And, plagued by physical infirmities since childhood, he was sensitive to any hint of weakness. FB

Karen Knorr’s languid photograph, part of a series of 26 images she took in gentlemen’s clubs in Mayfair, London, captures how comfortable certain men feel luxuriating in hereditary privilege – “an archetypal image of aristocratic power”, in Knorr’s words.

Each photograph is paired with a satirical text written by Knorr, who was inspired by parliamentary speeches and books about the British empire. “I wanted to make work that used irony and parody to explore attitudes prevalent amongst the English establishment in the 1980s,” she said. FB

Russian president Vladimir Putin has a penchant for staging topless photo ops – always while partaking in a macho outdoor activity such as horse-riding or hunting. “It is easy to laugh at,” says Ruth Ben-Ghiat, author of a book on the political figure of the strongman from Mussolini (who also liked to pose shirtless) to the present. “But the use of masculinity as an authoritarian tool is deadly serious. Strongmen use their bodies to proclaim themselves the defenders of the nation, and yet they often pose as victims as well.” GS

“A vital element has been added to the well-planned and generously financed campaign to make Senator Jack Kennedy president of the United States,” reported the North American Newspaper Alliance in 1957: the Kennedys were expecting their first child, Caroline.

A year later, Life magazine staff photographer Ed Clark visited the couple’s family home in Georgetown. Clark later recalled that when asked if he could take a photo of the senator with the baby, “Jackie said no, that she was upstairs asleep. But Jack bounded up the stairs, and I followed.”

Jackie ended up asking for 75 copies of “that marvellous picture” to give to family and friends. And after JFK became president in 1961, the framed photo was hung in the Oval Office. His identity as a father of small children had become a key part of his public image as a novel breed of male politician: the youthful and vigorous leader of – to borrow his well-known phrase – “a new generation of Americans”. GS

This famous shot of a naked aeroplane gunner was captured by Horace Bristol, who was part of a group of photographers recruited to promote US naval aviation during the second world war. The aircraft had been sent to rescue a US marine pilot shot down while attacking Japanese forces at Rabaul Bay in the Pacific.

“One of our crew stripped off his clothes and jumped in … He couldn’t have swum very well wearing his boots and clothes,” Bristol later recalled. “As soon as we could, we took off.” Though the soldier has never been identified, his image quickly became a symbol of male valour and heroism in wartime. GS

“He was a dandy and a great eccentric,” remembered Leigh Bowery ’s friend Donald Urquart in 2004, “in the tradition of Curricle Coates, Bunny Roger, Barbara Cartland, Edith Sitwell, and Quentin Crisp.” As a performance artist and “club kid” of the 1980s, Bowery’s intricately constructed – and sometimes controversial – outfits and costumes exploded traditional ideas of what a man could look like and what he could do.

In one famous performance, he birthed his friend and later wife, Nicola Bateman, out of a “vagina”, with an umbilical string of sausages trailing behind. Another was seen by painter Lucian Freud, who immediately asked Bowery to sit for him.
Bowery died in 1994 at 33 of an Aids-related illness. “I miss him,” friend and film-maker John Maybury said last year. “He was like a kinetic beacon, vibrating.” FB

Adrian Street went by many nicknames, including “the Exotic one”, “the Sadist in Sequins” and “the queen bitch of pro wrestling”. His catchphrase was, “Imagine what I could do to you,” finished with a suggestive, moaning, “ Mmm …”

In the 70s, the Welsh former coalminer became famous for his taunting, butch, queer-coded persona. For a profile in a national tabloid in 1974, he arranged this striking photograph – much reprinted over the years – down his former pit with his miner father, who had disapproved of his career.

“That look, even though it’s outrageous, he would have said it was super-masculine,” says artist Jeremy Deller , who made a film with Street before his death in 2023. “It’s a challenge, isn’t it? You’re challenging other people as well as society, so you have to back it up.” FB

“It’s fake violence, a parody,” said William Klein of his 1954 photograph. “I asked the boy to point the gun at me and look tough. He did, and then we both laughed.” Klein saw the image as a “double self-portrait”; he himself was a mix of “the street kid trying to look tough, and the timid good little boy on the right”.
Klein saw it as playful, but the twisted face of the child retains a threatening power. FB

This photograph – actually a still from a newsreel – was first published in Life magazine in 1941, to illustrate the fall of France after the Nazi invasion. As the Germans advanced, the French government decided to send the historic regimental flags of its armies to safety in Africa. Before they were put on ships out of Marseille, a parade was held through the streets of the town. It was here that cameraman Marcel de Renzis caught footage of a French citizen called Jerôme Barzetti weeping as they passed by.

The image is often cited as a rare example of public tears from a man, as taboos around male emotional expression have softened in recent years. A 2016 study found that modern men cry in public more than twice as often as their fathers. Barzetti’s tears, however, fit into a long history of martial crying, with roots in Homeric epics. According to one count, men are depicted weeping in the Odyssey more than 30 times. FB

“The most wonderful specimen of man I have ever seen” is how a Harvard professor described Eugen Sandow upon taking his measurements in the 1890s. By then, the Prussian-born athlete was a global fitness star. Today, he is remembered as the father of modern bodybuilding, having organised the world’s first major “physique” competition in London in 1901. “He’s Arnold Schwarzenegger before Arnold Schwarzenegger,” says sports historian Conor Heffernan.

As Heffernan explains, Sandow’s “lean and muscular physique” – still aspirational now – had previously been more associated with farmers and sailors than the perfect man. Images such as this helped to reinforce what modern bodybuilders refer to as the “Grecian ideal”: a physical type based on statues from the ancient world. (Although appearances can be deceiving, as Heffernan points out: the dumbbell Sandow is lifting is probably empty.) GS

In Ralph Ellison’s novel Invisible Man, the unnamed narrator, an African-American man, hides out in a basement in New York, which he lights with 1,369 bulbs. “Before that I lived in the darkness into which I was chased, but now I see. I’ve illuminated the blackness of my invisibility – and vice versa,” he says, before telling the story of a life that had, until then, been defined by ideas projected on to him due to his race and gender.

Gordon Parks collaborated with Ellison on A Man Becomes Invisible, a photo essay published in Life magazine to promote the book. The striking images recreate key scenes from the narrative; this one shows the final passage, in which the protagonist (played by John Bates, an actor friend of Ellison’s) emerges from his underground retreat through a manhole – a reclamation of his place in society. GS

“You can show two men killing each other at three in the afternoon in any country in the world on public television,” said photographer Wolfgang Tillmans in an interview in 2022 . “But you can’t show two men kissing each other.” Ghetto was a cult London venue of the noughties; at a club night there called The Cock, Tillmans captured a tender, passionate moment between two men. When the photograph was exhibited in Washington DC in 2007, one visitor reacted by slashing it with a key. It’s since become a symbol of solidarity and resistance: after the shooting at Orlando’s gay nightclub Pulse in 2016, many posted Tillmans’ photograph as a defiant act of protest. FB

In this photograph, David Bowie is captured pushing a pram with his baby, Zowie, alongside then wife Angie. Laura King, a historian of modern Britain, explains its significance: “In the decades after the second world war, there was a real movement towards what I call family-oriented masculinity. Men often weren’t doing anything like what women were doing in terms of looking after children, but fatherhood was very much aligned with masculinity.” Pushing a pram became a way to signal your identity as an involved family man.
Bowie – the famously gender-bending icon – wasn’t exactly a typical dad of his time. “I don’t feel very paternal,” he told an interviewer in 1976 . GS
“Ballet is woman,” proclaimed the choreographer George Balanchine. The idea that it’s a dance form for girls persists today, especially in cultures where machismo is dominant.

Against this backdrop, Uruguayan photographer Santiago Barreiro documents the diversity of men’s ballet in Latin America. For Barreiro, his subjects offer an example of how traditional gender roles – which he has observed as deeply ingrained in Latin societies – can be deconstructed through art.

This portrait depicts Juan Pablo Rodríguez, a Colombian-born choreographer and principal soloist with the Ballet Nacional del Perú. Rodríguez told Barreiro that he sees freedom of expression as an act of resistance. GS

Hugh Hefner ’s urbane, sex-obsessed vision of masculinity “became central to what it meant to be a modern man” in the 1960s, says historian Amber Batura. Hefner would spin Playboy magazine – first published in 1953 thanks to a loan from his mother, among others – into a global empire of clubs, staffed by women wearing distinctive “bunny” uniforms.

Like Ian Fleming’s James Bond, Hefner modelled a fantasy of masculinity “as gratifying, masterly play”, in the writer Esther Allen’s words, “in which women were seen as a sort of consumer product”. As Hefner put it himself in 1992: “Much of my life has been like an adolescent dream of an adult life.” FB

“Black men from the third world have not previously revealed either to their own peoples or to the west a certain shocking fact,” wrote the Nigerian photographer Rotimi Fani-Kayode in 1988. “They can desire each other.”

After training with the US photographer Robert Mapplethorpe in New York, Fani-Kayode moved to London and produced a stunning body of work from his Brixton home studio, before his death from Aids-related complications in 1989.

Mark Sealy, co-editor of a new book of Fani-Kayode’s work released this month, calls it a “radical transformation of Black male subjectivity”, made at a time when “the Black male subject was wrapped up in violent hostility via the press as muggers and bad guys”. Fani-Kayode’s work presented a subversive and playful vision of queer Black masculinity “at the height of Aids, in a very, very homophobic society”. FB

“The virtue of all-in wrestling is that it is the spectacle of excess,” wrote Roland Barthes ; wrestlers are performers in a pantomime of rivalry and aggression. This photo depicts one of the most celebrated bouts of all time: the hotly anticipated face-off between Hulk Hogan and André the Giant (also known as Fezzik from The Princess Bride ) at WrestleMania III in 1987. Pro wrestling had boomed in popularity and the stakes were raised by a much-publicised feud between the superstars, who were actually good friends. Hogan defeated a 520-pound (37 stone) André with his legendary “bodyslam that was heard around the world”. GS

Over the course of his 50-year career , Martin Parr repeatedly trained his camera on the football stadium – though, as a committed chronicler of ordinary British life, he was less interested in the players and more in the fans. In this photograph from 2012, we witness a moment of unbridled euphoria for the supporters of Wolverhampton Wanderers, who have just scored in a home match at Molineux stadium.

“[Football fandom is] a way of people accessing emotions. It’s very tribal,” Parr said when interviewed in 2022 . “It’s an important aspect of creating your own identity. Especially for men; it’s a very welcome way of letting your emotions go.”

There is a dark side, too; recent statistics show that racist and homophobic abuse are on the rise at matches, and there was once again a spike in domestic violence reports during this year’s World Cup . GS

The actor Billy Porter is known for his audacious, gender-fluid red carpet fashion. “This look was interesting because it’s not drag,” he told Vogue of this gown, which he famously wore to the Oscars. “I’m not a drag queen. I’m a man in a dress.” Inspired by a Renoir painting, and made at short notice in over a week of 18-hour days by designer Christian Siriano, Porter’s tuxedo dress garnered huge attention, coming just a month after he wore a bright pink cape to the Globes, which in his words “changed everything for me”. The dress was later displayed in the Victoria and Albert Museum , and has its own (extensive) Wikipedia page . FB

“I decided to shoot pictures of men who made comments to me on the street,” Anderson wrote of her 1973 series titled Fully Automated Nikon (Object/Objection/Objectivity). The artist displayed the images with white strips over catcallers’ eyes, granting them anonymity while also symbolically taking away their ability to objectify her. GS

“Growing up in Morocco, we were definitely not scared of colour,” Moroccan-British photographer Hassan Hajjaj has said. His playful portraits blend north African textiles with markers of global consumerism; his sitters often wear clothes designed by him.

This image was part of Hajjaj’s recent My London Rockstars series featuring portraits of artists in the capital, including Our Motherland Collective, a skateboarding crew that has transformed into an arts group.

“The people in the pictures come from all different parts of the world, and when you start putting them next to each other, it becomes a positive image,” Hajjaj has said of his work that explores identity and multiculturalism. If his photos make a young person think, “Oh I can be that person,” or, “I can be the person taking that picture,” he says, “that’s the greatest feeling you can have as an artist”. FB

“I had a personal motivation to establish an Indian gay presence in art history,” says the artist and photographer Sunil Gupta , who was born in New Delhi in 1953; he later settled in London in the 1970s. “It was hard for me to be postmodern because I had no references. So I decided to make the references.” He wanted to “visualise” the experience of gay men in Delhi.

Initially, “nobody wanted to be in the picture” – homosexuality in India wasn’t decriminalised until 2018 . Eventually, Gupta was introduced to a network of gay men who agreed to model for the project Exiles (1986–87). The accompanying texts came from interviews he’d conducted at cruising sites around the city. GS

This year marks the 40th anniversary of one of the bestselling posters of all time: a photograph of a hunky man cradling a baby. Paul Rodriguez, art director of the poster retailer Athena, conceived the idea and recruited photographer Spencer Rowell. The image tapped into the archetype of masculinity that emerged in western culture in the 1980s: the New Man, who rejected sexist ideas around domesticity.
The model is Adam Perry, who later claimed to have leveraged the poster’s fame to sleep with more than 3,000 women – not quite a New Man, after all. GS

“Ever since that picture of a pregnant man was sprung on an astonished nation,” wrote a Daily Mirror columnist in 1970, “we men haven’t been able to stop wondering what would happen if we really did become pregnant.”
The public information poster, dreamed up by ad company Cramer Saatchi, caused a storm when it was released, aimed at increasing the “sexual responsibility of the male”.
Photographer Alan Brooking, now 98, remembers an extended search for the perfect model – a man in possession of “the subtle kind of embarrassment that one might expect in that situation”. FB

“It is like a resistance movement for peace,” journalist and photographer Justin Makangara says of the sapeurs. “They are fighting with clothes.” The sapeurs of the twin Congolese capitals of Brazzaville and Kinshasa have become famous for their style.

Until recently, many regarded the sapeurs as “foolish, hooligans, idiot people” for spending so much money on flashy clothes. Recently, however, Makangara has seen a change in their public perception. Most sapeurs – like Celestin Moundounga, the 48-year-old technician here – hold down respectable jobs and are “responsible to the needs of their families”. And as the civil war grinds on in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, their way of life suggests that “even in conflict, we can try to be in joy”. FB

It was the 1998 World Cup in France, a peak moment for British lad culture. Then David Beckham was photographed wearing a Jean Paul Gaultier wrap. The Sun ran the photo alongside the headline “Beckham has got his Posh frock on”.

The footballer has stood by the look. “Sarongs are great,” he said in 2014 . “I would still wear it now.” Today his bold outfit is recognised for cementing Beckham’s role as the poster boy for a new type of heterosexual male ideal: the fashion-forward metrosexual of the 2000s. GS

Thomas Dworzak was on a photographic assignment covering the fall of the Taliban when he stumbled on a set of highly stylised studio portraits of soldiers of the former regime in a photo shop. The fighters had probably died before they could pick them up.

“I was very surprised, of course,” he says. The Taliban had famously banned all photography of living beings. He bought the prints – the beginning of a collection eventually published in the 2003 photobook Taliban .

In the secretly commissioned portraits, the fighters pose against pastel-coloured and scenic backdrops and hold props such as flowers and guns. Here, two men clasp hands. The unmistakably “camp aesthetic”, Dworzak explains, was “not specific to the Taliban” – such images can be found across the region. But they also couldn’t be further from what we expect a militant soldier to look like. GS

The sight of a man with a baby strapped to him was too much for Piers Morgan in 2018 , who posted this picture with the hashtag #emasculatedBond. Men responded in their thousands with photographs of themselves similarly “emasculated” – including wrestling star Adam Copeland holding his child while dressed as Elsa from Frozen. “Any man who wastes time quantifying masculinity,” tweeted actor Chris Evans at the time, “is terrified on the inside.” FB

The clashes that arise between differing factions of masculinity could be summed up by this photograph of a brawl between mods and rockers in Brighton in 1964. That summer, long-standing tensions between the competing youth subcultures erupted in a series of confrontations during bank holiday weekends in seaside towns across the south of England.

It’s now thought that the extent of the fighting was overplayed at the time – a moral panic stirred up by the establishment about the youth of the day. But the rivalry was real enough. The rockers, who rode high-speed customised motorcycles known as “cafe racers”, mockingly compared the Italian scooters of the “sissy” mods to their “mums’ hairdryers”. As one mod put it to a BBC interviewer at the time: “You can’t just stand and let a load of kids take the mick out of you, can you?” GS

Hells Angels – the motorcycle gang founded in California – haunted the US psyche in the 1960s. They modelled a rebellious, hyper-masculine image, but were also – for the time – provocatively homoerotic, frequently giving each other “a sloppy wet kiss”, in writer Hunter S Thompson’s words. “It blows their minds,” said one Hells Angel of the effect on “squares” – “especially the tongue bit”. FB

An interest in “performing masculinity” – which she first explored in San Francisco’s butch lesbian community in the 1990s – eventually led photographer Catherine Opie to high school football. Her portraits of star players, taken just after practice, show “adolescent boys beginning to form and perform for the first time an image-ideal of manhood”, in the words of one critic.

Opie also linked the series to the various wars that the US was involved in at the time. “So many young men were having to make very interesting choices between sports scholarships and becoming a soldier,” she has said. “It was actually very emotional.” FB

Historically, pubs and other drinking places were considered a “masculine republic”, somewhere for the menfolk to gather while their wives stayed at home. The notion of the watering hole as an almost exclusively male space – with notable exceptions granted to barmaids, landladies and loose women – is summed up in this image of an establishment in the working-class Gorbals district of Glasgow in 1968.

German-born Schadeberg , best-known for his portraits of life in South Africa under apartheid, had been sent to the Gorbals to document an area in rapid transition: the old tenements were being pulled down and replaced by modernist housing. GS
“I had let down the fans, my team-mates, the manager, everybody,” remembered Paul Gascoigne in 2020. “I cried because I thought it was the end of my career.”

In 1990, 23-year-old Gazza had already captured the hearts of the public for his skill in the World Cup. When he burst into tears after receiving a yellow card for tackling a West German player, the nation erupted with a mixture of sympathy and, eventually, mockery. Today, public male tears are a relatively uncontroversial part of major sports tournaments, with everyone from Tiger Woods to Roger Federer having a good sob. FB

Which people, places, or problems do you expect this article to mention?

Masculinity is important in this story because ______.
The article mentions image to explain ______.

Introduction by Luke Kennard I have an image of myself in 2011, pushing my newborn son in a big red buggy because he would only nap when in motion.
As I traversed the streets of suburban Birmingham, I felt observed, glanced at, commented on in a manner that ranged from pity to reproach to disproportionate admiration.
The article says masculinity is unrelated to the main events described.
The article says nothing in the situation affects people, places, or decisions.

What does the article say about masculinity?

What question would you ask after reading the details about image?

articles.title: Tim Dowling: a literary festival in Greece doesn’t inspire much hope – and sadly, nor do I
articles.summary: In between talks on geopolitical doom, one woman says I put her off journalism, while another thanks me for doing the same for her son I’m at a literary festival in Greece, standing by some sort of colonnade, drink in hand, fulfilling my role as a non-luminary. Ahead of me, hands are being shaken and warm words exchanged. The sun has just set, and there is a faint glow coming off various luminaries. “Why are you just standing there?” my wife says, coming up behind me. Continue reading...
articles.content:
In between talks on geopolitical doom, one woman says I put her off journalism, while another thanks me for doing the same for her son

I ’m at a literary festival in Greece, standing by some sort of colonnade, drink in hand, fulfilling my role as a non-luminary. Ahead of me, hands are being shaken and warm words exchanged. The sun has just set, and there is a faint glow coming off various luminaries.

I’ve been to lots of literary festivals without my wife, where I spend a lot of time either in my hotel room or in a dark corner of the opening drinks thing. At some point I’m usually required to give a talk, and then I go home. I do not, at any point, give off any light.

But I’m not even doing a talk at this festival; I’m just here to play in the band. We did it last year and we’ve been asked back. But we aren’t playing until the penultimate evening, and in the meantime my schedule is full: swim, rehearse, attend talks outlining different forms of geopolitical doom, lunch, swim.

“There are people you know from last year,” my wife says. “You can’t stand behind a tree all night.”

The next day I’m drinking a coffee between events, staring at the sea and thinking about geopolitical doom, when a woman comes up and introduces herself. She reminds me that I once gave a talk at a university where she was a journalism student. This would have been about 15 years ago. It was possibly the first time anyone had asked me to give a talk about anything, and I remember being both inept and a little graceless.

Anyway, she didn’t become a journalist as a result of my uninspiring words – she now manages cycling tours, one of which, it turns out, I’ve been on.

“Fine,” I say. “We’re all doomed, but in the meantime I think I’ve signed up for a second cycling holiday.”

That evening I go online and track down a contemporary student report of the university talk I gave 15 years ago. “He referred to himself as a ‘frightened little man’,” it reads. I’m struck by how long I’ve been committed to this version of myself.

I attend half a dozen more talks promising imminent extinction. The penultimate evening comes, and the band plays to a big crowd on a pier looking out to sea. The next morning people stop me in the street and at the talks to express their appreciation. For a moment I get a faint idea of what it must be like to give off a little light.

At the end of the final lunch a woman introduces herself and tells me I once gave her stepson a day’s work experience on a journalistic assignment exploring urban wildlife. This would have been 25 years ago.

I had contacted various guides and arranged to meet them in different parts of London where secret and exotic wildlife could be found: rare birds, insects, plants and bats. I did research, made lists and planned a route.

The day before, I received a parcel containing a full safari outfit, which I was to wear in all the photographs. That, it turns out, was the assignment.

When the appointed morning arrived, it was raining and freakishly cold for July. I feared the safari outfit would mean the guides wouldn’t take me seriously, but it was worse than that: they thought I wasn’t taking them seriously. They were not happy. I was not happy. The photographer was not happy, and my work experience person was miserable.

“There wasn’t really much for him to do,” I tell the woman. “But I made him carry my pith helmet because I refused to wear it on the tube.”

On the wall of my office there is a framed photograph of me dressed in that stupid safari outfit, rain dripping off the pith helmet, pretending to look through binoculars. The caption reads: “Anyone Seen My Dignity?”

Every time I look at it I think of the poor work experience person, standing off to the side, shivering in the drizzle and holding my butterfly net.

“Anyway, after spending the day with you, he decided he didn’t want to be a journalist,” says the woman. “So I just wanted to thank you.”

At the end of that day I decided I didn’t want to be a journalist either, but it was too late.

Every time I look at it I think of the poor work experience person, standing off to the side, shivering in the drizzle and holding my butterfly net.
“Anyway, after spending the day with you, he decided he didn’t want to be a journalist,” says the woman. “So I just wanted to thank you.”
At the end of that day I decided I didn’t want to be a journalist either, but it was too late.

articles.content:
On Saturday Night Live last week, comedian Shane Gillis made a pathetic ‘joke’ about the clothes women wear to the gym. It was puerile – but also pernicious

I ’ve spent the morning doing Shane Gillis’s work: checking out women in the gym. If you’ve avoided Gillis thus far, apologies for enlightening you – he’s a “comedian” who recently told a “joke” on Saturday Night Live that began: “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dressed like whores now.”

Well, reporting for duty from the weight room, here’s the clothing tally: eight women in leggings and T-shirts; six in T-shirts and trackie bottoms; five in shorts and vest tops; one in a crop top and leggings. It’s not exactly the Folies Bergère – there’s not much, I would have thought, to cause Gillis to blush. But maybe I’m wrong – how undressed, exactly, constitutes whorish? Is a glimpse of a female forearm a distracting provocation? Should we pull up our socks to avoid inflaming male passions with our slutty ankles when we’re doing step-ups?

There’s a long, grim history of women trying to do physical activity in appropriate clothes and not being allowed, or feeling able to. We might not be sweating in floor-length dresses and corsets like early Olympian women , but bros are still complaining about girls doing squats in shorts in their eyeline, staring, propositioning and commenting (the #gymcreep hashtag is a veritable rogues’ gallery of them). Even Gillis’s language isn’t, unfortunately, exceptional: after his monologue, fitness writer Mikala Jamison shared a message on her Substack from a man she considered a friend, saying a gym had “whores everywhere”.

Thigh-rubbing lechery around women’s workout gear, however jokey, is gross and infuriating, but it’s more pernicious than that. Women get alienated from sport and fitness when they’re not allowed to feel comfortable in their bodies and clothes: research by the England hockey player Tess Howard found that many girls were put off sport because of clothing requirements and concerns around sexualisation, while Women in Sport found more than 1 million girls in the UK “fall out of love” with sport in their teenage years. Women are less active than men, with 38% still not doing 150 minutes of exercise a week . When girls and women are deprived of, or never allowed to develop, a sense of ease and enjoyment around having a body in public, this is the result.

I say “enjoyment” specifically because that’s something I think gets left aside in making the inarguable, entirely correct, case that what women wear to work out for comfort, practicality or ease of movement, is nobody’s business but their own. But what about pleasure? Gyms are many things – a refuge, a third space, a repository of crimes against music – but they’re also a place to enjoy your body, including how it looks.

I know, because going to the gym made me feel good about (bits of) mine for the first time since puberty. I was the one in the crop top this morning, flaunting my stretchmarks, hernia and distended belly button, yes, but also the results of two years’ hard work. I’m proud I can lift a wardrobe now, but I’m also proud to look a bit pumped. It gives me confidence: enough to walk into strange weight rooms full of men wherever I happen to be and do my thing. Those experiences in turn have shown me that most gym-goers of both sexes aren’t remotely interested in what anyone else is doing, or wearing – they’re working on (maybe admiring!) themselves.

But I’m 51, and my experience of the gym isn’t the same as it is for younger women. Sport England research published this summer found 19% of women aged 16-34 felt uncomfortable or unsafe in fitness centres because of the possibility of harassment or intimidation; 86% reported experiencing physical, verbal, non-verbal or online harassment or intimidation in a fitness or leisure centre in the last three years. This kind of comment feeds the fear, and emboldens aggressors, making it not just unfunny, but depressing and enraging. Everyone should be able to enjoy moving their body unmolested, that’s a given. But dammit, we should also get to enjoy wearing short shorts, second-skin leggings and spaghetti-strap tops. To look safely and happily in a gym mirror and find ourselves, yeah, a bit fit.

articles.title: Desiree Miller runs rampant to inspire Wallaroos to eight-try rout of Scotland
articles.summary: WXV: Australia 56-12 Scotland at Accor Stadium Miller becomes first Wallaroo to score 20 Test tries Desiree Miller created some neat history as the Wallaroos hit top gear in a 56-12 defeat of Scotland in Sydney. Shifted to full-back, the speedster scored tries from near-identical plays off scrums as Australia scored 42 consecutive points in a Saturday lunchtime banquet at Accor Stadium. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Desiree Miller created some neat history as the Wallaroos hit top gear in a 56-12 defeat of Scotland in Sydney.

Shifted to full-back, the speedster scored tries from near-identical plays off scrums as Australia scored 42 consecutive points in a Saturday lunchtime banquet at Accor Stadium.

With her opening try Miller became the first Wallaroo to have scored 20 Test tries.

Scrum-half Samantha Wood pulled the strings and kicked well while Randwick winger Amelia Whitaker scored her maiden try and Maya Stewart crossed on return from an Achilles injury.

The eight tries to two victory, in the Wallaroos’ first Test on home soil since April, followed their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh last month that broke a run of six Test losses.

Scotland scored first when Katie Buchanan latched on to a long ball and cut back inside to create a 5-0 lead.

But the Wallaroos settled and, after threatening to barge over on multiple occasions, eventually found joy with a try to hooker Brittany Merlo.

That breakthrough opened up the Scottish defences and the Wallaroos picked it apart with another five tries inside the next 30 minutes of play.

Scotland eventually fired a shot through Rachel Malcolm but Whitaker bobbed up again with a sharp intercept and blazing long-range effort to score her second try.

Eva Karpani, also back from injury, then capped the Wallaroos’ dominant day with a rampaging try, dragging three defenders over the line on the buzzer.

The match was the first course of a historic quadruple header on Saturday, with Australia’s sevens men’s and women’s teams also set to play before the Wallabies face the All Blacks later on Saturday.

articles.title: Masterplan review – Stanley Tucci is wasted in Amazon’s smooth-brained heist caper
articles.summary: A ‘family’ of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thriller In the last half-decade Stanley Tucci has been a source of near-inexhaustible on- screen delight, whether making friends with nonnas in his delightful cooking shows or smartly judged supporting turns in Conclave and The Devil Wears Prada 2 . He is an actor well placed for a star vehicle of his own, and this one, Masterplan , sounds good on paper: an art heist fronted by the actor at his most debonair, flanked by a grandson of a French New Wave legend (Victor Belmondo, related to Breathless star Jean-Paul) and a buzzy breakout of The White Lotus (Simona Tabasco, winning in season two of Mike White’s comedy). There’s a good bit of pulpy fun to have here, with double, triple and quadruple crossing, silly spy gadgetry which has been updated to include retina scan cloning and something called “VR intrusion”. As British criminal mastermind Roger, Tucci is game to send up aristo archetypes, even if his character often veers into parody. “I’m English,” his character says at one point. “‘Not bad’ is what I say when I orgasm.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
A ‘family’ of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thriller

I n the last half-decade Stanley Tucci has been a source of near-inexhaustible on- screen delight, whether making friends with nonnas in his delightful cooking shows or smartly judged supporting turns in Conclave and The Devil Wears Prada 2 . He is an actor well placed for a star vehicle of his own, and this one, Masterplan , sounds good on paper: an art heist fronted by the actor at his most debonair, flanked by a grandson of a French New Wave legend (Victor Belmondo, related to Breathless star Jean-Paul) and a buzzy breakout of The White Lotus (Simona Tabasco, winning in season two of Mike White’s comedy).

There’s a good bit of pulpy fun to have here, with double, triple and quadruple crossing, silly spy gadgetry which has been updated to include retina scan cloning and something called “VR intrusion”. As British criminal mastermind Roger, Tucci is game to send up aristo archetypes, even if his character often veers into parody. “I’m English,” his character says at one point. “‘Not bad’ is what I say when I orgasm.”

Just as you settle in for an evening of will-they-won’t-they hijinks, the film pulls a bait and switch. It turns out that the pair have been set up by Roger (Tucci), a veteran thief himself who has the “job of a lifetime” for them: a decade-in-the-making plan to make off with the Mona Lisa in a complicated scheme that involves drones, trickery, truffle-related espionage and a long-forgotten tunnel that conveniently exists under the Louvre. Also: they are in fact brother and sister, the result of an energetic mid-90s for Roger when he seduced their respective mothers.

You would think the fact that they are now siblings would put the kibosh on Jay and Chiara’s flirtation, but the film seems to feel otherwise. As the makeshift family relocate to Paris to put plans in motion for the heist, Chiara makes jokes about the size of her half-brother’s “hammer” and offers to settle squabbles through a round of strip poker, which strikes me as an unusual way for siblings to bond.

Despite the jokes that land with a thud, Masterplan is on safer ground when it sticks to the espionage. That is thanks to Thomas Vincent, the director, recapturing some of the juice he showed in the episodes of Bodyguard he directed, and I would rate Masterplan as a hair better than Role Play , the dull film he previously made for Amazon. When it isn’t trying to dazzle you with technology, Masterplan has a few twists on heist movie tropes (including a very clever use of a helium balloon) that avoids it feeling like a total retread of the Ocean’s 11 franchise, even if it doesn’t come close to matching the ingenuity of those films. And while the characters are too thinly drawn to make you care too much about them, I appreciated flourishes that nod to the female and gay male gaze, such as the diva moment where Tabasco’s character dons a platinum blond wig and the camera’s lustiness for Belmondo, who has a talent for losing his shirt.

Everything isn’t as it seems, and while the film should really end 30 minutes before it does, it has a few final tricks up its sleeve in the third act, as the characters begin to learn who they can really trust and Chiara’s hacking skills are put to the test once more. Even as the plot becomes increasingly ridiculous, ample bangs and explosions ensure that the nearly two-hour runtime doesn’t totally drag. The best you can offer Masterplan is faint praise: it could breeze by as company to your Sunday night takeout even if you will struggle to remember it a week later.

articles.title: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
articles.summary: The 28-year-old detained by German police is accused of being part of the cyber-crime gang that hacked blood-test firm Synnovis in 2024.
articles.content:
The alleged Qilin hacker Vladimir K. was detained upon arrival in Frankfurt

German police have detained a Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang which caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death.

The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death.

The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates.

Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime.

The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K.

He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday.

According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country.

He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims.

Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency.

While his extradition was first reported in early October , external , the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations.

Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab.

A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere.

King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly" .

A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result".

"The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time.

A similar attack in 2020 by a different hacker group on a hospital in Düsseldorf in Germany led to a negligent homicide investigation being opened after an elderly patient died.

It was later dropped after medical experts concluded the patient's condition was so severe that they would have died regardless of the issues caused by the cyber-attack.

Prosecutors could also not definitively prove that it was the direct cause of death.

In total, the Synnovis hack in 2024 disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption.

The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom.

The hackers refused to answer any more questions once challenged by the BBC

The criminals eventually published the highly private data online after no ransom was paid.

At the time, they told the BBC the hack was not just for the money but to protest the UK's lack of help in the Russian war on Ukraine .

But the hackers did not say if they were from Russia or Ukraine, and their claims were dismissed as an attempt to distance themselves from the cyber-crime extortion tactics Qilin were known for.

The group, which has been tracked since 2022, is behind a string of criminal hacks targeting schools, hospitals, companies, councils and health organisations.

It was also behind the high profile and disruptive hack on Japanese beer maker Asahi in October 2025.

It is very rare for hackers to be arrested in Russia as its government refuses to co-operate with Western law enforcement requests.

The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death.
The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates.
Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime.
The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K.
He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday.
According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country.
He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims.
Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency.
While his extradition was first reported in early October , external , the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations.
Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab.

A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere.
King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly" .
A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result".
"The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time.
A similar attack in 2020 by a different hacker group on a hospital in Düsseldorf in Germany led to a negligent homicide investigation being opened after an elderly patient died.
It was later dropped after medical experts concluded the patient's condition was so severe that they would have died regardless of the issues caused by the cyber-attack.
Prosecutors could also not definitively prove that it was the direct cause of death.
In total, the Synnovis hack in 2024 disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption.
The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom.
The hackers refused to answer any more questions once challenged by the BBC
The criminals eventually published the highly private data online after no ransom was paid.
At the time, they told the BBC the hack was not just for the money but to protest the UK's lack of help in the Russian war on Ukraine .
But the hackers did not say if they were from Russia or Ukraine, and their claims were dismissed as an attempt to distance themselves from the cyber-crime extortion tactics Qilin were known for.
The group, which has been tracked since 2022, is behind a string of criminal hacks targeting schools, hospitals, companies, councils and health organisations.
It was also behind the high profile and disruptive hack on Japanese beer maker Asahi in October 2025.
It is very rare for hackers to be arrested in Russia as its government refuses to co-operate with Western law enforcement requests.

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s new press secretary: ‘attorney in the way George Santos was volleyball champion’
articles.summary: Late-night host discussed Trump’s falling poll numbers and concerns over his new press secretary, Katie Zacharia Trump’s new press secretary says it’s ‘unknown’ how much she’ll deal with media With other hosts still on holiday, Jimmy Kimmel checked in on Donald Trump ’s record-low poll numbers and beleaguered new press secretary , Katie Zacharia. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Late-night host discussed Trump’s falling poll numbers and concerns over his new press secretary, Katie Zacharia

Trump’s new press secretary says it’s ‘unknown’ how much she’ll deal with media

With other hosts still on holiday, Jimmy Kimmel checked in on Donald Trump ’s record-low poll numbers and beleaguered new press secretary , Katie Zacharia.

“We are only 19 days away from our president claiming that the elections were rigged,” said Kimmel on Thursday evening. “Never mind the fact that he is the one trying to rig them, of course.

“Republicans got some very bad tidings from the fake liberal media,” as even the president’s former favorite, Fox News, predicts that Democrats will flip the House in the midterms.

The network “also betrayed Daddy” with a new poll that said his approval rating is now at 36%, its lowest point ever, while traffic to Trump’s social media site, Truth Social, is down 30% year to year. “He seems to be the only one who posts to Truth Social,” said Kimmel. “And I seem to be the only one who reads those posts on Truth Social. It’s really just the two of us.

“Don Jr hasn’t posted on Truth Social in two months,” he added. “Even Eric hasn’t posted since July. His own stupid sons have forsaken him!

“But people are still showing up by the dozens to see him in person,” the host continued. “Trump has been touring and boring the country all this month, to remind voters what an amazing job he thinks he’s doing, and to castigate the fake news for not turning the cameras around to show the size of his crowds.”

At one of his rallies on Thursdays, Trump pursued such a point in his usual nonlinear fashion and wondered: “Is the camera like, statutory? Is it like a statue, you cannot move it?”

“Statutory – it’s a word he learned from his best friend Jeffrey Epstein ,” Kimmel joked.

In other Trump news, the president announced that he would be cancelling Pete Hegseth ’s plans to livestream a military execution by firing squad, because there are “many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die”.

The execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army major and psychiatrist who shot and killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood in 2009, was set for 3 December. But Trump “had second thoughts after realizing that the man they would be executing is in a wheelchair”, Kimmel explained. “I guess he realized he’d have a hard time selling ads on a live stream of a paralyzed man being executed by firing squad, and what’s the point if he can’t make a little bit of money on it, right?

“I wonder if he’ll show the same kind of mercy to his new future former press secretary,” Kimmel quipped, referring to Zacharia, Trump’s new press secretary whose first week on the job was less than stellar.

On Thursday, the former fringe network commentator tried to set the record straight on questions about her status as an attorney , and “it turns out that Katie Zacharia is an attorney in the same way George Santos was a volleyball champion ,” Kimmel quipped. Zacharia has yet to confirm when or where she passed the bar exam; the Wall Street Journal reported that Zacharia failed the California bar exam after graduating from law school there in 2011.

“His press secretary is supposed to be answering questions about his lies, not hers!” Kimmel added. “But the truth is, he didn’t hire her to be his lawyer. He didn’t really hire her to be his press secretary. He hired her so he could squeeze into a helicopter with her and Natalie” – Harp , his fellow blond assistant – “and rub his cankles against a woman’s legs without getting cursed out in Slovenian.”

articles.title: Add to playlist: the buzzy bildungsromans of boy wonder Superfan and the week’s best new tracks

articles.content:
Kali Flanagan was handpicked by Julian Casablancas to support the Strokes – now, at 21, he’s writing songs full of the rushing emotions of youth

From New York Recommended if you like Cameron Winter, Adrianne Lenker, Alex G Up next My Piledriver Heart album out now; UK tour beginning 4 November

Making coming-of-age music as a young person can feel strange after a pandemic. So here are a few more curveballs. Imagine the breezy, youthful indie you post online in your early teens gets you a record deal. Covid happens. You move to New York, change your artist name, and then Julian Casablancas eyes you at an open mic and invites you to open for the Strokes in Colorado, aged 18, solo.

This pinball game of life is the music career of Superfan, AKA Kali Flanagan, who is now 21 and whose latest album, My Piledriver Heart, offers up a codex of miniature bildungsromans worth the buzz.

Flanagan’s primary tools are some of the simplest: drop-tuned, condensed acoustic guitars (which he calls “acousticellos”) and quietly strong vocals reminiscent of Elliott Smith or Alex G. Roomy drums and distortion on tracks such as In the Gold Room or Keeping Your Smile add a welcome noisy edge.

The album’s true power is Flanagan’s ability to hand-spin emotion out of simple melodies, phrases or builds, thanks in part to deft cello work by Omeed Almassi (who has also played with Bar Italia): take the way the strings mimic an unfurling guitar line at the climax of Miss W Jones , or the bassy Nick Drakeian outro to Ode to Hum (I Want It to Rise) . Even so, when you think Flanagan lands on something concrete, he doesn’t: this is music that conjures up new feelings on every listen. Isn’t that what growing up is all about? Archie Forde

@​ – Love in the Dark The Philadelphia duo , who in a previous generation might have been dubbed freak-folk, release their album Autosmile today, and it’s one of the year’s very best. This particular track has a riveting blend of innocence and experience, with hymnal yet careworn vocals.

Snoh Aalegra – Karma An utterly stunning, minimalist R&B ballad with shades of Maxwell to its chorus and mk.gee to its guitar, as Aalegra lacerates herself over the way she betrayed a lover.

​Blondie – Spectral Eyes Though Johnny Marr wrote it and plays the big, simple riff, the lead single to the New York legends’ first album in nine years is all about Debbie Harry, rhythmically chattering through the chorus with a rough, time-worn grade to her voice.

Carissa’s Wierd – I Don’t Feel Like I Feel Right In the 25 years since their last album, the US indie duo have amassed a huge audience on streaming who will no doubt flock to this new single, a romantic tussle whose tension is kept taut even as the epic drums kick in.

Marla Kether – Libera (ft Margaridas) Her day job is being Little Simz’s bassist, but Kether’s own music is well worth seeking out: Libera is a propulsive Latin-house track with delicate, chirrupping vocals by Margaridas – and, predictably, a killer melodic bassline.

Teri Rini – Behind Every Mirror You can reliably smash “buy now” on anything Melbourne label Efficient Space puts out, spanning contemporary artists and crate-digging comps. This, a spellbinding 1981 song from an overlooked US jazz singer, is from an upcoming example of the latter, entitled Nothing Ever Was.

Post Common – Check Atomiser Guitars are rarely as gorgeously distorted as they are here, with tones like a wind-assaulted microphone shifting through the Brighton trio’s otherwise melodic post-hardcore.

articles.content:
The director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and grief

T aika Waititi detonates an explosion of postmodern quirkiness and ironic dorkiness in this unbearably mannered, unspeakably acted film. It’s a slice of sentimental whimsy-futurism and non-satire, adapted by Waititi from the Kazuo Ishiguro novel, which winds up saying nothing substantial or meaningful (or funny) about artificial intelligence, love or grief. Klara and the Sun is soft-centred sci-fi-lite, simultaneously demanding we laugh at its (unfunny) humour and wipe away a tear at its pass-agg poignancy. With earlier films like Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Thor: Ragnarok, Waititi showed he can do comedy. But this, sadly, is closer to his notorious fey-Hitler fantasy Jojo Rabbit – misjudged and self-admiring.

In the world to come in an uncanny valley of the almost-real, families can buy “artificial friend” or AF robots for their kids. In terms of tech plausibility overall, incidentally, their status isn’t entirely clear: AF salesperson (Natasha Lyonne) says that the recent third world war has wiped out the internet. (This post-WW3 world looks in pretty good shape apart from that.) And these AF humanoids incidentally have a kind of purple blood called PEC-9 running through them which one character incidentally tells us is “highly flammable”. (Uh-oh. Quite the design fault.)

One such AF is teen girl Klara, played by Jenna Ortega as a ditsy, cutesy, supremely lovable innocent: a manic pixie dream robot – only nice – who is solar-powered and who therefore, in her adorable childlike robot way, worships the sun as a god. But Klara is an earlier, more rudimentary AF model, less sophisticated and robust apparently than the newer upgrades which run on Bluetooth as opposed to solar. (Is that really better?)

At all events, her flaws are presented as analogous to the vulnerabilities of the human teen who wants Klara; this is Josie (Mia Tharia), a 14-year-old genius-prodigy who has been expensively “lifted” into a super-IQ class via a new surgical procedure, but who is also very lonely and suffering from an unspecified illness. Her uptight mom is played by Amy Adams and the grumpy housekeeper Melania – whose appearance is the nearest the film comes to comedy – is played by Rachel House. Klara goes to live with her new family in their distant home in a weirdly dreamlike Midwest farming landscape from which the city can only be glimpsed distantly, like Oz. Klara becomes certain that the sun lives in the nearby barn above, from which she can see it rising every morning; what a sweetly naive belief. And so it goes on, to a twist ending that is as unsatisfying and contrived as everything that has gone before.

The thought of robots or replicant youngsters having real intelligence or real feelings is a difficult subject; Hirokazu Kore-eda came unstuck with the idea of robot child replacements in his recent film Sheep in the Box . Kogonada’s parable After Yang , about AI child robots, was a more interesting and persuasive movie. But this is a sentimental and laborious mess.

articles.title: ‘Children are naturally drawn to beauty’: the head of the ‘Issey Miyake’ preschool on their pleated uniforms

articles.content:
Ms Lam Montessori’s head of school reveals teachers wear a different Japanese designer after their chic clothes drew online envy

“D oes anyone know what the deal is Ms Lam Montessori … and why all their employees wear Issey Miyake … every day … I’m confused and a bit jealous,” asked one commenter on the Williamsburg subreddit last week, sparking a unexpected viral moment for a chain of Brooklyn Montessori preschools.

The poster was responding to photos on the Montessori’s website of the teachers’ uniforms: raspberry, cobalt and apple green dresses in plissé fabric. They appeared to be from the Pleats Please line by Japanese designer Issey Miyake. It seemed an avant-garde choice for staff posing in front of the abachi and blond wood toys of their preschool classroom.

On X, those pictures were screen grabbed and viewed 3.5m times, with most comments reading along the lines of “only in Brooklyn”.

Over email from Taiwan, Ms Lam Montessori head of school, Stephanie Woo – a vision in chartreuse pleated fabric and matching hexagonal-framed glasses on the nursery’s website – explains that the dresses are actually by a more affordable Japanese designer, Yamasaki Takashi (they are priced around a 10th of the $700 one might pay for a Pleats Please frock), and are worn at all of the company’s locations. Ms Lam is a Mandarin immersion school and was originally founded in Taipei, Taiwan, where it has 14 branches, as well as its five in Brooklyn.

Woo is herself a “huge fan” of Issey Miyake, and owns “a couple of pieces that I bring out for special events at the school”. She adds: “Issey Miyake clothing is of course stunning, but we chose Yamasaki for its understated designs, comfort, durability and price. Those qualities made it a particularly good fit for everyday life in our classrooms,” she writes, adding that the clothes wash well and “hold their color and shape beautifully. Even after we’ve washed it 100 times, they still come out of the dryer looking much the same.”

She adds that the outfits were originally her mother’s idea – the original Ms Lam – who, according to the company’s website, was the first person to bring Montessori to Taiwan. Staff in Taiwan have been wearing them for 12 years and in Brooklyn for eight. Uniforms are important, she says, working with children from the age of one to six: “They help a young child recognize, even on a busy campus, this adult can help me.”

One of the reasons the Issey Miyake-esque outfits so delighted the internet is that the Pleats Please line, which launched in 1993, is having a fashion resurgence.

One particular garment – the Madame T stole, a large piece of plissé fabric with a diamond-shaped neck hole, which comes with an instruction booklet for the many ways it can be folded around the body – has recently become a social media fascination . In August, the shopping platform Lyst ranked it among the hottest products of the summer, and reported a 100% rise in demand for Issey Miyake quarter-on-quarter.

That said, Issey Miyake – which was launched in 1970 in Tokyo – and its more affordable Pleats Please line has never really been uncool. Miyake was the first of the wave of Japanese designers – followed by Yohji Yamamoto and Rei Kawakubo’s Comme des Garçons – to break through into European fashion.

Miyake developed his then revolutionary near-permanent pleats in the late 1980s, by constructing garments first, flat, at a much larger size than they would eventually fold down to, then heat-pleating afterwards. Most Pleats Please garments are 100% polyester, and their popularity comes despite a larger polyester backlash . Unlike fast-fashion polyester, Pleats Please are high quality, the designs timeless – and the construction of the garments makes specific use of polyester’s thermoplastic properties to hold shape, rather than using cheap polyester to make throwaway knockoffs of natural fibers.

Pleats Please’s practical, technical and arty associations – the focus is on the garment, and its own silhouette, rather than the body beneath – has made it popular with accomplished creative women for decades. Zaha Hadid, Solange Knowles, Meryl Streep, Tessa Thompson and Joni Mitchell are among its longtime fans, while Lorde, who wore a neon pink Pleats Please crop top at Lollapalooza Doja Cat have been spotted wearing the designer more recently.

In the west, says Dr Sasha Raspopina, the course leader for the fashion marketing and journalism BA at London Metropolitan University, Pleats Please has a kind of “if you know you know” appeal. She has noticed its adoption in east London among young people, who are perhaps “trying to signal that they are creative”. Given that context, Raspopina thought the Montessori image was a meme at first because the garment seemed to speak of an “alternate universe” to that of the kindergarten teacher.

The use of a Pleats Please-inspired garment may land differently for an east Asian audience, says Prof Wessie Ling, a visiting professor of transcultural arts and design at the University of Bologna (who, as a fashion scholar, knew the dresses weren’t genuine Miyake the moment she saw the photo: “the materials, and how it drapes on the body isn’t quite there,” she says).

She says that the link between Japanese design and Taiwan is very deep, given the colonial history (Taiwan was under Japanese colonial rule from 1895 until 1945). In east Asia more broadly, she says, there is a profound “admiration for Japanese designers, specifically the first generation of Japanese designers”. Miyake was the first to open a boutique in Paris, in the 1970s, nearly 10 years before Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto. This was at a time when “absolutely no other non-white designers made it into the fashion capital. So he represents something.” In east Asia, she says. Miyake is “the signature Japanese designer” and the first designer brand a woman would turn to if they reached executive level.

Ling had not heard of the brand Yamasaki Takashi , but she has noticed many younger, independent east Asian designers, including those based in South Korea and Vietnam, recently using pleats similar to Miyake’s. She doesn’t necessarily consider them to be copycats. “Obviously it is a kind of Miyake because it’s pleats – but they also create different patterns, colors and silhouettes, and they are putting some thought into the pleats they are trying to create.”

As Woo adds over email, the aesthetic of the garments certainly matters, even at school: “The truth is, we believe young children should be surrounded by beauty. From birth to age six, children have what Montessori calls the ‘Absorbent Mind’ – they effortlessly absorb so much from their surroundings,” she says. “They are naturally drawn to beauty, and by making it part of their daily lives, we hope to nurture their appreciation for it and their desire to care for the spaces and things around them.”
